name: Serratia bacterial leaf spot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed Cannabis bacterial disease producing small vein-limited angular lesions that can coalesce across leaves, stems and flower parts. Red bacterial ooze is useful supporting evidence, but neither lesion shape nor red material is species-confirmatory; plant-linked isolation and molecular identification are required.
affectedParts: leaves | leaf veins and interveinal tissue | stems | flower parts | whole aerial plant in severe greenhouse observations
stages: vegetative | flower | greenhouse production; original report | field or other production context not established
indicators: Small dark-brown 1–3 mm lesions are angular or vein-limited on hemp leaves | Early lesions are localized around veins rather than uniformly circular | Lesions coalesce into larger irregular necrotic regions as disease advances | Compatible injury can extend from leaves to stems and flower parts | Red bacterial ooze or streaming can emerge from affected tissue, including after a lesion is punctured | Dark-pink raised colonies and Gram-negative bacilli were part of the original isolate description | 16S rRNA plus rpoB sequence evidence supports Serratia marcescens rather than a visual bacterial-leaf-spot label | Reproduction of compatible lesions after inoculation, symptomless controls, and reisolation provide pathogenicity support
exclusions: Angular or vein-limited lesions are present without plant-linked bacterial isolation or molecular evidence | Red, pink, or sap-like material is present without microscopy, culture, and plant linkage | Round dark-margined lesions with gray-brown centers and pepper-like fungal sporulation support Exserohilum | Pycnidia or another fungal fruiting structure support Septoria or another fungal leaf spot | Xanthomonas or another bacterial pathogen is identified from the same lesions | Lesions remain confined to an exposure edge or spray/contact pattern and no organism is recovered | Mite or thrips organisms and feeding signs explain stippling, silvering, bronzing, or scarring | Only detached, stock, vendor, forum, generated, or low-resolution imagery is available without collection and laboratory metadata
lookAlikes: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot | Other bacterial leaf spot or blight | Exserohilum / Helminthosporium leaf blight | Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Anthracnose | Downy mildew / Pseudoperonospora | Thrips or mite feeding injury | Contact spray, droplet, or mechanical injury | Marginal or interveinal nutrient injury | Mixed-pathogen leaf spot
confirmation: Capture the intact plant, canopy distribution, affected organs, both leaf surfaces, lesion scale, vein relationship, and a close-up of any ooze before sampling. | Sample several fresh, active lesion margins with intact plant identifiers; retain matched asymptomatic tissue and environmental/exposure history as controls. | Use aseptic bacterial isolation and record colony morphology, but do not identify Serratia from pink or red pigment alone. | Use Gram reaction/microscopy plus validated molecular identification; the original report used 16S rRNA and rpoB sequence evidence. | When causal ground truth is required, link the same plant and lesion sample to pathogenicity evidence or an equivalent qualified plant-diagnostic conclusion, not merely an environmental isolate. | Investigate fungal fruiting structures/spores and other recovered organisms because hemp leaf diseases overlap and mixed infections can occur. | Keep symptom-only, angular-lesion-only, red-ooze-only, detached-leaf, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed Serratia class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Separate strongly affected propagation material and avoid moving wet symptomatic tissue through clean areas. | Preserve fresh, plant-linked lesion samples before sanitation or treatment and photograph sampling locations. | Avoid manipulating or puncturing suspect lesions outside an appropriate diagnostic workflow.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed bacterial-disease sanitation and management appropriate to the production system; visual appearance alone does not justify a Serratia-specific intervention. | Correct documented splash, sanitation, or leaf-wetness risks without treating those conditions as proof of pathogen identity.
prevention: Sanitize tools and contact surfaces between plant groups and minimize splash movement from symptomatic plants. | Use clean propagation material and retain lot/plant identifiers through diagnostic sampling. | Scout leaves, stems, and flower parts together so multi-organ progression is documented rather than reconstructed from isolated close-ups.
warnings: Serratia includes strains of human-health relevance; use appropriate hygiene and qualified diagnostic-laboratory handling. | Angular necrotic lesions, red ooze, and pink-red colonies are supporting observations, not species-specific ground truth. | The original report was greenhouse-bound and included cultivar Carmagnola; do not generalize its timing, severity, distribution, or cultivar response. | The NC State hemp image is a generic bacterial leaf spot/blight differential with no explicit species-level caption, item-level creator credit, reusable license, or linked laboratory record; it must remain hidden from display and training.

name: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot
summary: A documented bacterial leaf spot of hemp in which small water-soaked lesions progress to approximately 1–2 mm necrotic centers surrounded by comparatively broad yellow halos; images can support triage but cannot distinguish the bacterium from fungal or abiotic look-alikes.
affectedParts: leaf blades | upper and lower leaf surfaces
stages: growth stage not established in cannabis-specific primary evidence
indicators: Small water-soaked leaf spots before necrosis develops | Necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter | Yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide | Discrete lesions with a halo wider than the necrotic center | Focal spotting rather than a whole-leaf nutrient-mobility gradient
exclusions: White surface colonies, fungal fruiting structures, or diagnostic spores support a fungal cause | Fine stippling, webbing, or organisms on the leaf underside support arthropod feeding | Damage follows spray droplets, contact points, or a documented chemical application and does not progress after exposure ends | Symptoms follow a measured older-leaf or younger-leaf nutrient pattern without discrete water-soaked lesions | A plant diagnostic laboratory identifies another pathogen or abiotic cause from a representative active lesion
lookAlikes: Septoria or other fungal leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Foliar spray injury | Edema or water-soaking from physiological stress | Thrips or mite feeding punctures | Localized nutrient or salt injury
confirmation: Photograph the whole plant and both sides of several leaves, then capture a scale-referenced close-up showing the necrotic-center and halo dimensions and the distribution of lesions across the canopy. | Submit fresh, recently expanding lesions that include the transition between healthy and affected tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory; keep samples separate, cool, and dry according to that laboratory’s instructions. | Ask the laboratory to distinguish bacterial from fungal leaf spot and, if a Xanthomonas isolate is recovered, identify it with validated physiological and molecular or sequence-based methods rather than morphology alone. | Microscopic bacterial streaming may support a bacterial differential, but absence of streaming does not exclude bacteria and streaming does not confirm Xanthomonas cannabis to species. | Map reports using the current accepted name Xanthomonas cannabis while retaining Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis as a historical synonym for literature and laboratory searches.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and pause movement of cuttings or symptomatic foliage until laboratory triage. | Handle suspect foliage only when dry, avoid splash between plants, and clean hands and tools before moving to unaffected plants. | Keep unconfirmed lesion photographs out of bacterial ground-truth and training sets.
correctivePlan: Base removal, sanitation, and any crop treatment on the confirmed diagnosis and local legal label; a visual bacterial-leaf-spot suspicion is not a treatment prescription. | Inspect nearby plants for comparable small haloed lesions and document whether new lesions appear after splash or handling events without treating that association as proof. | If laboratory results do not recover or identify the bacterium, reopen fungal, arthropod, chemical, and physiological differentials.
prevention: Use documented healthy propagation material and retain lot or mother-plant traceability. | Minimize leaf wetness and splash during routine handling where compatible with the production system. | Disinfect tools and segregate symptomatic material under a written sanitation protocol.
warnings: A photograph or video cannot confirm Xanthomonas cannabis; lesion size and halo geometry are triage features only. | The key symptom measurements come from a historical Japanese hemp report and do not establish current local prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, or production-system risk. | General greenhouse bacterial-leaf-spot guidance is used only for differential diagnosis and handling precautions, not as cannabis-specific epidemiological proof. | No cannabis-specific image or video with verified reuse and automated-training permission was found for this batch; no media was copied or admitted.

name: High-temperature or high-light exposure
summary: Measured high temperature or unusually intense light can alter Cannabis physiology, yield, and flowering development, but published Cannabis experiments do not validate cupping, bleaching, or a single PPFD or temperature value as a universal visible injury diagnosis.
affectedParts: whole canopy | upper and lower inflorescences | recently expanded leaves | canopy nearest a local heat or light source
stages: vegetative | flower initiation | flower development | late flower
indicators: Air temperature, leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, and humidity are recorded at the affected canopy position across time | Abnormal new inflorescence clusters develop on top of older inflorescences during sustained high-temperature flowering exposure | Flower maturation or production differs from a matched cultivar under a cooler measured regime | Gas-exchange or chlorophyll-fluorescence measurements change even when a specific foliar lesion is absent | A spatial gradient repeats with measured temperature or irradiance rather than merely with leaf age
exclusions: No time-stamped canopy-level temperature, leaf-temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, or humidity record supports an exposure event | Only upward leaf curl, pale tissue, dry margins, or canopy posture is visible | Mites, thrips, webbing, cast skins, eggs, frass, or feeding scars are present | Root-zone water content, irrigation history, pH, EC, or root disease explains the distribution better | The change follows nutrient, pesticide, growth-regulator, or other chemical application | Only late-flower senescence or cultivar-typical inflorescence architecture is visible | High PPFD alone is treated as injury even though the plant is acclimated and temperature and water status are within its measured response range
lookAlikes: Water shortage or excessive vapor demand | Potassium deficiency | High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability | Hemp russet mite | Broad mite | Thrips injury | Wind or fan injury | Pesticide or plant-growth-regulator injury | Normal late-flower senescence | Cultivar-typical foxtailing or inflorescence architecture
confirmation: Map PPFD and air temperature at multiple canopy positions and times; measure leaf temperature with a calibrated contact or infrared method and record humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, photoperiod, carbon dioxide, and lamp distance. | Compare affected and unaffected plants of the same cultivar, developmental stage, irrigation treatment, and root-zone condition; include a cooler or lower-exposure reference when available. | Inspect leaf undersides and protected new growth with magnification for mites and thrips, and document the root system, substrate water content, pH, and EC. | Use serial whole-plant, canopy, and close-up images with an exposure log; do not convert a single photograph or uncalibrated camera color shift into heat- or light-stress ground truth. | For abnormal flowering, inspect multiple inflorescences over time and compare with cultivar records to separate heat-associated reversion or foxtailing from normal architecture, late-flower growth, or genetic traits.
immediateActions: Preserve the pre-correction environmental log and matched photographs, then remove an acute unsafe heat load or equipment fault gradually. | Verify irrigation delivery and root-zone moisture before changing light, humidity, or irrigation together. | Quarantine or isolate only when pest or infectious disease evidence warrants it; environmental exposure alone is not contagious.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured source, such as a canopy hot spot, failed cooling or air mixing, excessive lamp proximity, or an abrupt unacclimated light increase, while changing one controllable factor at a time. | Re-map the canopy after correction and score only new tissue and subsequent inflorescence development against a matched control. | Escalate persistent abnormalities to pest microscopy, root-zone testing, tissue analysis, or a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly reducing light without evidence.
prevention: Log canopy-level PPFD, photoperiod, air and leaf temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, and irrigation status by zone. | Map hot spots and irradiance gradients after fixture, HVAC, canopy-height, or density changes. | Retain cultivar- and stage-matched healthy reference sequences because published temperature optima and production responses vary among Cannabis genotypes.
warnings: Upward curl, tacoing, bleaching, pale tops, dry margins, and leaf angle are nonspecific and are not validated Cannabis heat- or light-stress ground truth without measured exposure and exclusion checks. | A controlled Stillwater trial produced linearly increasing inflorescence yield through 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second; therefore PPFD magnitude alone does not prove injury or define a universal damaging threshold. | Temperature optima for photosynthesis differed among tested drug- and fiber-type varieties, so 25, 30, 35, or 40 degrees Celsius must not be generalized into one cultivar-independent diagnosis. | The abnormal inflorescence-cluster observation came from defined 31/27 degrees Celsius flowering treatments in two genotypes and should be labeled treatment-associated, not universally heat-specific. | No reusable Cannabis symptom photograph with exposure measurements and adequate causal confirmation was admitted in this record; media remain empty rather than promoting anecdotal or vendor imagery.

name: Herbicide injury — clomazone-type bleaching
summary: An exposure-confirmed hemp differential for Group 13 clomazone injury. Compatible new-growth bleaching is highly nonspecific: a clomazone label requires a temporally and spatially plausible soil-carryover, pre-emergence, or vapor-drift pathway, ideally strengthened by records or residue analysis.
affectedParts: newly expanding shoot-tip leaves | young leaves | older foliage later in sustained injury | seedlings and young transplants | whole plant secondarily
stages: emergence | seedling | young transplant | vegetative | established plant after off-target drift
indicators: The youngest expanding leaves or shoot tips become pale green, pale yellow, or nearly white while older pre-exposure foliage may initially retain more green pigment | Pigment loss can be interveinal, marginal, patchy, or nearly complete rather than following a single Cannabis-specific shape; occasional pink-to-purple margins may occur in sensitive non-Cannabis plants | Affected tissue may remain bleached and growth-reduced, advance to necrosis under severe exposure, or be followed by normally green new growth after a limited exposure | Several Cannabis plants share a boundary, downwind, previous-crop, treated-soil, bed, container-lot, equipment, or irrigation-source pattern rather than a random single-leaf pattern | Susceptible weeds or other plant species near the same field edge may show compatible pigment loss, strengthening a vapor-drift hypothesis without proving the active ingredient | A documented commercial hemp field case linked clomazone soil carryover to bleaching of newly formed tissue and nonrecovery | A controlled pre-emergence greenhouse screen found severe stand, height, and biomass reductions in Felina 32 hemp at the tested clomazone rate, establishing hemp sensitivity under those conditions
exclusions: No plausible clomazone or related pigment-inhibitor source, timing, route, field history, neighboring application, equipment pathway, or residue evidence can be established | Iron, sulfur, manganese, root-zone pH, EC, water status, or tissue results explain the leaf-age and canopy pattern better | Bleaching is restricted to the most light-exposed canopy surface or lamp footprint and measured irradiance or heat history supports photooxidative injury | Stable sectoral or clone-recurrent variegation persists without an exposure gradient, growth suppression, or injury progression | Magnification finds broad mites, hemp russet mites, thrips, feeding scars, eggs, cast skins, or webbing linked to the affected tissue | Discrete lesions, surface growth, ooze, vascular discoloration, root/crown disease, or validated pathogen testing supports an infectious cause | Rapid droplet-shaped scorch, bronzing, or near-immediate necrosis fits a contact or PPO-inhibitor exposure better than carotenoid-inhibitor bleaching | Color loss disappears under neutral calibrated lighting or is attributable to clipping, white balance, overexposure, compression, or infrared imaging
lookAlikes: Severe iron deficiency | Sulfur deficiency | Manganese or root-zone pH disorder | High-light or heat bleaching | Genetic or chimeric variegation | Broad mite or hemp russet mite injury | Thrips feeding injury | Pseudomonas or another bleaching infection | Contact-herbicide injury | PPO-inhibitor bronzing / scorch | Other carotenoid-inhibitor herbicide injury | Camera white-balance or exposure artifact
confirmation: Capture neutral-color whole-area video plus matched upper, middle, and lower canopy stills, close-ups of both leaf surfaces, and unaffected comparison plants before any correction. | Map affected and unaffected Cannabis plants against field edges, wind direction, previous-crop rows, treated soil, bed or container lots, irrigation zones, traffic routes, and application or transplant dates. | Photograph susceptible weeds and other plant species along affected and unaffected edges; shared bleaching supports an exposure plume but does not identify clomazone. | Reconstruct product, active ingredient, rate, formulation, application, weather, soil, prior-crop restriction, equipment-cleanout, substrate, and water-treatment records with a qualified crop professional. | Preserve plant, soil, water, and product samples under an accredited laboratory chain of custody when residue analysis is appropriate; interpret nondetection with sampling time, analyte, matrix, and method limits. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, moisture, and temperature and obtain plant tissue analysis where appropriate to test nutrient and root-zone alternatives. | Inspect growing tips with magnification and submit plant-linked tissue for pathogen testing when pest or infectious differentials remain plausible. | Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, non-Cannabis, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and exposure-unlinked samples out of the confirmed clomazone class and automated training.
immediateActions: Stop further suspected exposure without disturbing evidence; preserve labels, spray and field records, weather data, equipment-cleanout history, and representative samples. | Segregate suspect plant lots and prevent contaminated soil, substrate, water, tools, or equipment from moving into unaffected production areas. | Do not apply speculative nutrients, pesticides, or flushing treatments before documenting the pre-correction pattern and root-zone measurements.
correctivePlan: Base any response on the confirmed exposure route, residue context, plant stage, local pesticide law, and qualified agronomic guidance; this diagnostic record does not recommend herbicide use or a universal remediation. | Track the same plants and fixed viewpoints through later growth, recording whether green tissue resumes, bleaching progresses, necrosis develops, or plants fail to recover. | Investigate nutrient, light, pest, and pathogen alternatives concurrently when exposure evidence is incomplete or mixed.
prevention: Maintain complete pesticide, crop-rotation, field, substrate, water, and equipment-cleanout records and review legally applicable plant-back restrictions before hemp establishment. | Use drift-reduction, buffer, application-timing, and equipment-segregation practices required by the product label and local regulations. | Record baseline imagery and unaffected comparison areas so a later boundary or plume pattern can be evaluated.
warnings: Bleached Cannabis tissue cannot identify clomazone, dose, formulation, route, or legal source from appearance alone; photo/video confidence is capped at 0.20. | The controlled clomazone experiment tested one hemp cultivar, one greenhouse soil system, and one pre-emergence rate; its quantitative injury is not a universal Cannabis threshold. | The field nonrecovery case and institutional lighter-exposure recovery guidance describe different exposure contexts and should not be collapsed into a deterministic prognosis. | The two licensed NC State images show grape and pokeweed, not Cannabis; they are transfer references for color and field-edge context only and are excluded from Cannabis training and evaluation. | No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis clomazone progression image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch. | This profile is an injury-identification differential, not a pesticide recommendation or substitute for label, regulatory, laboratory, or professional advice.

name: Alternaria leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis brown-blight and leaf-spot differential supported by pathogenicity studies. Small dark or yellow spots, brown-to-gray lesions, halos, concentric rings, perforated centers, and black sporulation are compatible with Alternaria, but none is species-specific. Confirmed labels require plant-linked culture or validated molecular evidence; photo or video alone is capped at moderate-low confidence.
affectedParts: upper and lower leaf surfaces | leaf lesion centers and margins | petioles | stems | flower parts and buds | inflorescences | seed and propagation material as possible pathogen reservoirs | whole canopy for distribution context
stages: seed and propagation material | rooted cutting | vegetative | flowering | mature plant | field or controlled-environment production
indicators: Small dark or yellow spots develop on Cannabis leaves and enlarge into brown-to-gray lesions; the Chinese pathogenicity report described irregular brown lesions with light-yellow halos. | Compatible lesions may be circular or irregular, may have dark black-to-purple borders or yellow halos, and may show concentric rings, but any one of these patterns can be absent. | Lesion centers can become fragile or perforated as disease advances, creating a shot-hole appearance that is not unique to Alternaria. | Sooty black spore masses can develop in lesion centers, and affected leaf or bud surfaces can darken from brown toward brown-black as sporulation develops. | OSU field observations found some hemp spots about 0.1 inch or smaller, while more humid conditions can be associated with larger spots; size is contextual rather than a diagnostic threshold. | Alternaria-associated disease can involve leaves, petioles, stems, buds, inflorescences, or propagation material, so a whole-plant and organ-level sequence is more informative than a detached-leaf crop. | Repeated lesions associated with wet foliage, affected residue, or a wind/water spread pattern support a foliar pathogen pathway but do not identify Alternaria by themselves.
exclusions: Dark pycnidia embedded in lesions and laboratory evidence support Septoria rather than Alternaria. | Gray-brown sooty growth concentrated on corresponding lower-leaf lesions and Pseudocercospora morphology or sequence evidence support Pseudocercospora. | Round pale-centered lesions with melanized conidiophores and laboratory evidence support Cercospora. | Bipolaris, Colletotrichum, Exserohilum, Fusarium, Stemphylium, a bacterial pathogen, or another organism is recovered and linked to the sampled lesion. | Spots follow a spray boundary, droplet pattern, abrasion, heat/light exposure, or mechanical contact and do not continue to develop like an infectious lesion. | Chlorosis or necrosis follows a symmetric canopy/leaf-age pattern and measured pH, EC, moisture, or tissue data support an abiotic cause. | Punctures, stippling, frass, webbing, larvae, mites, or thrips account for the visible damage. | The only evidence is an unlinked detached leaf, stock image, generated image, vendor chart, or symptom description without a traceable sampled plant.
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot or blight | Anthracnose / Colletotrichum leaf spot | Exserohilum leaf blight | Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot | Fusarium foliar or flower blight | Stemphylium leaf spot | Bacterial leaf spot | Spray or contact injury | Thrips or mite feeding | Nutrient, pH, salinity, or water-stress necrosis
confirmation: Capture a traceable series from the same plant: whole canopy, upper/middle/lower canopy, both leaf surfaces, lesion-center macro with a scale, and any petiole, stem, bud, or inflorescence involvement. | Record plant ID, cultivar, stage, production setting, symptom-onset date, leaf or node age, recent wetness or irrigation events, nearby residue, environmental conditions, and any spray or mechanical exposure. | Before treatment, submit fresh representative lesion margins and, when relevant, affected petiole, stem, bud, or inflorescence tissue to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory. | Use culture and fungal morphology plus validated molecular identification from the sampled plant for an Alternaria organism label; preserve isolate and locus details when species-level resolution matters. | When multiple fungi or bacteria are recovered, require lesion linkage or pathogenicity evidence and keep the sample multi-label or unresolved rather than choosing the visually closest name. | Compare lesion progression with matched healthy plants from the same cultivar, stage, source group, and environment; absence of symptoms in appropriate controls strengthens but does not replace organism evidence. | Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, unlinked culture, mixed-organism, low-resolution, and stock/vendor/generated captures out of the confirmed Alternaria class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve representative untreated tissue and traceable photographs before removing heavily affected material. | Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending. | Map affected plants against irrigation zones, airflow, cultivar blocks, incoming plant lots, and residue sources.
correctivePlan: Use a disease-management plan appropriate to the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting. | Remove or contain confirmed diseased material and residue as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new lesions. | Evaluate response with new-growth and lesion-count records; old necrotic tissue will not become healthy after correction.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and do not move symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas. | Improve air circulation, limit avoidable leaf wetness, and manage infected crop or weed residue where feasible. | Scout both leaf surfaces and multiple canopy levels with consistent plant IDs so early spots can be followed over time.
warnings: Brown lesions, yellow halos, concentric rings, shot holes, and black sporulation are not individually specific to Alternaria. | Alternaria alternata and potentially other Alternaria species can affect Cannabis; a generic image cannot resolve species. | The two primary studies are regional and used specific isolates, tissues, and production contexts; prevalence, severity, and timing are not universal. | Alternaria can be recovered from seed or inflorescence material, but recovery alone does not prove it caused every visible lesion. | No image or video was added in this batch because no stable, item-level, panel-resolved Cannabis Alternaria asset with sufficiently clear reuse and training rights was verified. | All symptom-only, mixed-organism, detached, unlinked-laboratory, and low-resolution samples require human review.

name: Anthracnose leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot disease caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae. A Kentucky first report established a light-green-speck to tan-centered, dark-margined lesion sequence and fulfilled pathogenicity testing, while a later university survey only corroborated separate field occurrences. Photographs cannot distinguish it from other leaf-spot pathogens or physical injury.
affectedParts: leaf blades | leaf margins | lesion centers | adjacent leaf tissue when lesions coalesce | both leaf surfaces for paired documentation
stages: field-grown reproductive hemp in the first report | field research plantings | early lesion development | advanced coalescing lesions | diagnostic culture and pathogenicity testing
indicators: The reported sequence began with scattered light-green specks rather than an immediately open hole. | Developing lesions became round or angular and approximately 3 to 4 mm across. | Compatible lesions had tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos, but this color combination is not unique to anthracnose. | Lesion centers could crack and later drop out, creating a shot-hole or frog-eye appearance only after surrounding lesion development. | Multiple lesions could coalesce into larger necrotic regions rather than remaining isolated dots. | Lesions reaching a margin could be associated with marginal scorching, puckering, or twisting. | A useful image set pairs the full leaf and plant context with calibrated close views of intact early, developing, and center-loss lesions. | Compatible C. fioriniae culture morphology plus multilocus sequence evidence from the same lesion substantially strengthens the label; visual morphology alone does not.
exclusions: Physical holes, chewing, hail tears, handling damage, or training injury occur without a preceding discolored lesion, halo, or lesion-linked fungus. | Dark embedded pycnidia and a compatible laboratory result support Septoria leaf spot. | Gray-brown sooty or velvety lower-surface conidial patches support Pseudocercospora. | Tan-to-white centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophores and a compatible result support Cercospora leaf spot. | Concentric target-like rings or dark central sporulation with a compatible isolate support Alternaria as a differential. | Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a plant-linked bacterial identification support bacterial leaf spot. | A sharp spray, lamp, aisle, contact, or weather boundary without lesion-linked Colletotrichum evidence supports abiotic injury. | Culture, microscopy, multilocus sequencing, or repeated representative sampling identifies another organism or fails to link C. fioriniae to the lesions.
lookAlikes: Cercospora leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot complex | Alternaria leaf spot | Pseudocercospora olive / sooty leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Downy mildew | Bacterial leaf spot | Four-lined plant bug or other puncture injury | Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding | Hail, wind, handling, or training tear | Contact spray or herbicide injury | Edema or localized water-related tissue collapse
confirmation: Photograph the entire plant and canopy neighborhood, then both surfaces of several affected and unaffected leaves with a scale and stable plant identifiers. | Track the same intact early lesions through center cracking or loss; a single frame of an existing hole cannot establish the reported progression. | Collect multiple fresh lesions spanning intact early margins to developing centers before saprophytes obscure the lesion edge, following the receiving laboratory's packaging instructions. | Use lesion-edge culture and trained morphological examination to recover a dominant compatible Colletotrichum isolate, while recording other organisms recovered from the same tissue. | For C. fioriniae-level confirmation, require plant-linked multilocus sequence evidence comparable to the four-gene approach in the first report; do not assign the species from color, ITS alone, or a generic Colletotrichum image. | Where causality is uncertain or the isolate represents a new host or presentation, use pathogenicity evidence with symptom reproduction, reisolation, and symptomless controls. | Keep symptom-only, shot-hole-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and low-resolution samples out of confirmed training labels and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Tag and photograph representative plants before removing tissue, preserving the spatial pattern and lesion sequence. | Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and retain traceable fresh samples for a plant diagnostic laboratory. | Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, irrigation or splash zones, airflow, recent foliar applications, handling paths, and weather injury.
correctivePlan: Base disease management on the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting rather than on the anthracnose name or a photograph alone. | Contain or remove confirmed diseased material as locally appropriate and follow new lesion incidence on tagged plants; old necrotic tissue will not recover. | Reassess the diagnosis if new lesions do not follow the documented sequence or if repeated plant-linked tests do not support C. fioriniae.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic leaves, debris, tools, or splash water into clean production areas. | Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and retain adequate spacing and airflow where feasible. | Scout with stable plant IDs and matched full-plant, full-leaf, and macro views so early specks can be distinguished from later center loss.
warnings: Shot-hole, frog-eye, tan-center, dark-margin, yellow-halo, puckering, and coalescence features are not individually or jointly species-specific in a photograph. | The first report is a narrow Kentucky report; it does not establish national prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, universal canopy or leaf-age preference, infection timing, yield loss, or action thresholds. | The 2021 Kentucky survey only reports separate field occurrences and explicitly characterizes its findings as preliminary; it does not validate a camera-only label. | A Colletotrichum culture without plant and lesion linkage can represent incidental or secondary recovery and is not sufficient ground truth. | No image or video was indexed because no stable, item-level Cannabis anthracnose asset with clear reuse rights, plant linkage, and species-resolved confirmation was verified. | All symptom-only, hole-only, detached, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples require human review.

name: Bipolaris leaf spot
summary: A confirmed hemp leaf-spot and blight disease caused by Bipolaris gigantea. Necrosis can become severe, but lesion appearance overlaps Septoria, Cercospora, Alternaria, anthracnose, and abiotic damage.
affectedParts: leaves | canopy | buds secondarily when blight is severe
stages: vegetative | flower | field production
indicators: Necrotic leaf spots expand and can contribute to broader leaf blight | Disease can become widespread in outdoor hemp | Compatible lesions occur with Bipolaris conidia or molecular evidence from affected tissue
exclusions: Pycnidia dominate lesions | Cercospora-type conidiophores and white-centered round spots dominate | A chemical or physical injury pattern follows an exposure boundary | Laboratory testing identifies a different leaf-spot pathogen
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Anthracnose | Herbicide or contact injury
confirmation: Use fungal morphology and molecular identification from representative lesions for organism-level confirmation. | Record field distribution and lesion progression; one photograph is insufficient for B. gigantea.
immediateActions: Preserve symptomatic tissue for diagnosis before discarding representative samples. | Separate diseased material from clean propagation stock.
correctivePlan: Apply confirmed leaf-spot disease management appropriate to local rules and production conditions.
prevention: Reduce infected crop residue and prolonged leaf wetness where feasible. | Scout field plantings for early leaf spots.
warnings: Bipolaris leaf spot can look like several other Cannabis leaf-spot diseases. | Yield impact varies by cultivar, season, and disease complex.

name: Botrytis gray mold and bud rot
summary: A destructive Cannabis flower, stem, leaf, seedling, and postharvest disease associated with brown water-soaked or necrotic decay and, when conditions permit, gray to gray-brown sporulation. Internal flower decay can be poorly represented by an exterior view, and brown bud rot is not species-specific without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: developing and mature inflorescences | internal flower tissue | bracts and sugar leaves | stems and branch junctions | fan leaves under severe disease pressure | seedlings and cuttings | harvested and drying flower
stages: propagation | vegetative | flower | harvest and postharvest
indicators: One or more bracts or sugar leaves within a flower turn water-soaked, tan, or brown and collapse | Brown necrosis and mycelium occur inside a flower when it is carefully opened | Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth or dusty spore masses develop on dead flower or stem tissue under humid conditions | Localized flower decay expands until much or all of an inflorescence is brown, dry-rotted, or collapsed | Stem lesions become pale or brown cankers and may split, girdle, or break; black sclerotia can occur | Under severe late-harvest pressure, small circular leaf spots can enlarge, merge, and become vein-delimited necrotic areas, sometimes with yellow margins | Multiple affected flowers cluster in dense, humid, poorly drying canopy zones and increase on serial inspection

name: Cercospora leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease that often begins on older lower leaves as yellow flecks and develops into round lesions with pale centers, dark borders, and yellow halos. Conidiophore and laboratory evidence are needed because several pathogens make similar spots.

stages: vegetative | flower | late reproductive

correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-spot disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.

name: Exserohilum / Helminthosporium leaf blight
summary: A confirmed outdoor hemp leaf and stem spot disease. Round brown-to-black lesions with dark margins are compatible, but abundant conidia and laboratory identification are needed because the lesion appearance overlaps other leaf spots.
affectedParts: leaves | stems | canopy
stages: post-transplant | vegetative | flower | field production
indicators: Round brown-to-black lesions develop on leaves or stems | Lesions have distinctly darkened margins | Abundant large conidia can be observed within compatible lesions | ITS/RPB2 or equivalent fungal identification supports Exserohilum/Setosphaeria

lookAlikes: Bipolaris leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Bacterial leaf spot

correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-blight management and sanitation appropriate to the production system.

name: Fusarium foliar, flower and head blight complex
summary: A Cannabis Fusarium disease complex affecting leaves, flowers, drying floral material, stems and grain heads. It must be separated from Fusarium root/crown rot because infection site, symptom pattern and confirmation evidence differ.

stages: flower | reproductive | postharvest drying context
indicators: Floral surfaces develop abundant hyphae with light-brown necrotic tips | Leaves develop roughly circular light-brown lesions with darker brown margins and gray-brown aging centers | Blight is centered on floral/head tissue rather than beginning as root decay | Fusarium macroconidia, culture, sequence or species-specific molecular evidence accompanies compatible tissue

lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold / bud rot | Sclerotinia white mold | Alternaria leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Fusarium crown/root rot
confirmation: Submit representative fresh lesion/flower tissue for culture and molecular identification when Fusarium species matters. | For suspected F. graminearum, species-specific molecular assays can detect infection that is not yet visually obvious.
immediateActions: Separate suspect floral material from clean material and preserve diagnostic samples before treatment or disposal. | Inspect roots/crowns separately so root Fusarium is not conflated with foliar/flower blight.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-supported disease management and sanitation appropriate to the production stage and local crop rules.

warnings: Fusarium flower browning is not visually species-specific. | The 2020 survey identified both F. equiseti and F. graminearum in the foliar/flower blight complex; do not collapse every lesion into F. graminearum. | Image-only absence cannot exclude latent F. graminearum infection.

name: Powdery mildew
scientificName: Golovinomyces ambrosiae / Podosphaera macularis complex on Cannabis sativa
summary: Cannabis powdery mildew is a disease class marked by superficial whitish mycelium and conidia that expand across living foliage and sometimes stems or flowers. The phenotype can strongly support powdery mildew, but images cannot distinguish the documented Cannabis pathogens Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis.
affectedParts: upper leaf surface | lower leaf surface | petiole | stem | flower sugar leaf | flower bract or bud
stages: all | vegetative | flower | field production | indoor production

exclusions: Foliar spray or mineral residue often follows droplet edges or application patterns, may occur on nonliving surfaces, and lacks hyphae, conidiophores, and an advancing colony margin. | Normal glandular trichomes are regularly distributed structures anchored to floral tissue rather than irregular spreading white mycelial patches. | Spider-mite silk forms threads or sheets associated with mites, eggs, cast skins, and feeding stippling rather than a powdery fungal colony. | Botrytis produces advancing brown or water-soaked flower decay and gray-brown sporulation, often including internal tissue breakdown, rather than only superficial white colonies. | Downy mildew is associated with angular chlorotic-to-necrotic lesions and corresponding gray-to-purplish underside sporulation under wet or humid conditions. | Leaf bleaching, variegation, nutrient chlorosis, and camera overexposure remain within tissue and do not resolve into fungal hyphae and conidia under magnification.
lookAlikes: Foliar spray residue | Mineral or hard-water deposits | Glandular trichomes on floral tissue | Spider-mite webbing | Botrytis gray mold or bud rot | Downy mildew | Nutrient or root-zone chlorosis | Genetic variegation or camera artifact
confirmation: Do not assign a powdery-mildew species from a photograph or video. Capture whole-canopy distribution plus sharp upper- and lower-surface macros from several symptomatic and adjacent apparently clean leaves. | At the active colony edge, use magnification to document superficial hyphae and chains of conidia; include a scale and a gentle side-lit video or focus stack that separates fungal growth from residue and trichomes. | Record whether material transfers when touched, but do not use wipe behavior alone as confirmation because residue and fungal spores can both move. | For organism-level ground truth, submit fresh tissue to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and molecular testing; both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis are documented on hemp. | Record cultivar or genotype, plant age, growth stage, organ, canopy position, production setting, first-observed date, repeated fixed-area coverage, temperature, humidity, and recent foliar applications. | Treat absent colonies as a symptom-negative observation, not proof of resistance or pathogen absence; controlled resistance claims require replicated inoculation and appropriate susceptible controls.
immediateActions: Separate or flag affected plants, minimize handling and airflow disturbances that can disperse conidia, and preserve a fresh diagnostic sample before removal. | Map affected plants and organs, capture pre-intervention colony coverage, and inspect nearby plants on both leaf surfaces and flower-adjacent tissue.

prevention: Inspect incoming plants and clones under magnification and maintain cultivar/source identity so repeated susceptibility can be recognized. | Scout fixed leaves and flower-adjacent tissues across canopy zones, recording new colony area over time and retaining source-group identity for image sequences.
warnings: The 2019 Kentucky DOI originally identified Golovinomyces spadiceus; later taxonomy generally includes that name within G. ambrosiae. Preserve the original title and do not silently rewrite historical species labels. | At least two powdery-mildew fungi, Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis, have been PCR-confirmed on hemp, so disease-class imagery is not species-level ground truth. | The PM2 0-to-4 leaf-coverage scale is a controlled resistance-study scale, not a universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention threshold. | Cultivar, genotype, pathogen isolate, organ, plant stage, and inoculum pressure can change visible severity; adult plants in one study sometimes appeared more susceptible than their earlier clone assay. | The linked CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Figure 2 is a shared-experiment composite. It remains training-ineligible, and the resistant panel is not an independent universal negative sample. | Do not consume visibly mold-contaminated material, and do not apply unapproved products to Cannabis or flowering tissue.

name: Pseudocercospora olive / sooty leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease supported by a Thailand field collection and Koch-postulate experiment. Upper-surface olive, gray-centered, or pale vein-limited lesions paired with lower-surface gray-brown sooty sporulation are compatible with Pseudocercospora cannabina, but photographs cannot resolve it from other cercosporoid, fungal, or oomycete diseases. Confirmed labels require plant-linked morphology and molecular evidence.
affectedParts: leaf blades | upper leaf surface | lower leaf surface | vein-limited interveinal tissue | canopy foliage in severe disease
stages: field-grown vegetative or reproductive canopy | greenhouse plants near doors or vents | natural sporulating lesions | controlled inoculation
indicators: Natural field symptoms included circular-to-elliptical olive spots with gray centers and dark brown-to-black margins. | Upper-surface lesions can begin as inconspicuous or slight discoloration before becoming pale yellowish, irregular to subcircular, and approximately 2 to 6 mm across. | Lesions may remain bounded by veins, lack a sharply defined margin, and expand across a larger fraction of the leaf. | Corresponding lower-surface areas can be indistinct or pale yellowish rather than matching the upper-surface color exactly. | Grayish-to-pale-brown, velvety or sooty conidial patches occur chiefly on the lower surface and can follow veins. | Magnification may reveal conidiophores emerging in loose fascicles and pale olivaceous-to-pale-brown septate conidia, but morphology must be interpreted by a trained diagnostician. | Severe field disease was associated with defoliation; the institutional handbook also recognizes complete defoliation as a possible outcome. | In a controlled wet-box experiment, lower-surface stomatal penetration occurred within 24 hours and reproduced leaf spots with conidiophores and conidia at 5 days post-inoculation.
exclusions: Dark pinhead pycnidia embedded in lesions support Septoria rather than Pseudocercospora. | Tan-to-white round centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophores and a validated Cercospora result support Cercospora leaf spot. | Purple-to-gray underside growth with angular upper lesions and an oomycete result supports downy mildew. | White superficial colonies that wipe or scrape away and compatible microscopy support powdery mildew rather than a sooty hypophyllous leaf-spot mass. | Concentric rings, black central sporulation, or shot holes can support Alternaria as a differential but still require organism testing. | Mite stippling, webbing, eggs, or mobile mites without lesion-linked fungal structures supports mite injury. | A sharp spray, lamp, aisle, or exposure boundary with no lesion-linked structures supports abiotic contact, light, or chemical injury. | A plant-linked culture or molecular result identifies another organism, or repeated representative lesions fail to yield compatible Pseudocercospora evidence.
lookAlikes: Cercospora leaf spot | Septoria leaf spot | Downy mildew / Pseudoperonospora | Alternaria leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot or blight | Anthracnose / Colletotrichum leaf spot | Powdery mildew residue | Two-spotted spider mite injury | Bacterial leaf spot | Spray, contact, or light injury
confirmation: Capture the same attached lesion from the upper surface, lower surface, and whole-plant or canopy context; include a scale and record whether lesions follow veins. | Use a hand lens or microscope to determine whether lower-surface dark material is attached conidiophore/conidium growth rather than residue, insects, frass, or necrotic tissue. | Submit multiple representative, actively developing lesions with linked plant and location metadata to a plant diagnostic laboratory; do not base the result on a detached stock image. | Use fungal morphology together with validated sequence evidence; preserve locus, accession, isolate, and sampling details when assigning Pseudocercospora cannabina. | Prefer multilocus evidence such as ITS plus act, tef1, and rpb2 when species resolution matters because type-material sequence data are unavailable and morphology alone is difficult. | Where causality rather than detection is required, retain plant-linked isolation and pathogenicity or equivalent diagnostic evidence; organism detection alone does not prove every lesion was caused by it. | Keep symptom-only, upper-surface-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, and stock/vendor/forum/generated captures out of the confirmed Pseudocercospora class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph the distribution before removing tissue, then capture matched upper and lower leaf surfaces with a scale. | Preserve several actively sporulating lesions for laboratory diagnosis and limit movement of symptomatic leaves or propagation material. | Record indoor versus field context, greenhouse proximity to open doors or vents, recent wetness, and whether neighboring plants show a clustered or exposure-edge pattern.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation and environmental changes on a confirmed foliar-pathogen diagnosis and applicable local rules. | Track marked lesions and new foliage after intervention; disappearance of leaf wetness or sporulation does not retroactively confirm the species. | Escalate persistent or spreading lesions to a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly assigning a visual label.
prevention: Scout both leaf surfaces, especially in field plantings and greenhouse zones near doors or vents. | Improve air circulation, minimize avoidable leaf wetness, and remove infected leaves using sanitary handling. | Reduce carryover of infected crop residue where appropriate because the institutional handbook identifies residue as an overwintering pathway.

They are approved as references but excluded from automated training until panel crops, labels, source grouping, and rights metadata receive human review. | No photograph or video is ground truth without linked sampling and organism evidence; all symptom-only, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, and low-resolution samples require human review.

name: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
summary: A confirmed Cannabis Sclerotinia disease complex that can involve white-mold, crown-rot, wilt, and yellowing syndromes. S. sclerotiorum and S. minor are both documented on Cannabis/hemp; organism-level evidence is required because Botrytis, Fusarium, southern blight, and other molds overlap visually.
affectedParts: stems | crown | leaves | whole plant | flowering tissue depending on infection site
stages: vegetative | flower | all
indicators: White fungal growth occurs on symptomatic Cannabis tissue with associated wilt or yellowing | Affected tissue declines in a pattern consistent with an active stem/crown or aerial infection | Laboratory isolation or DNA evidence identifies Sclerotinia sclerotiorum
exclusions: Gray mold and laboratory evidence identify Botrytis | Root/crown testing identifies Fusarium or Pythium instead | White residue is nonliving spray/mineral material | No organism evidence accompanies nonspecific wilt
lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold | Fusarium wilt / crown rot | Pythium root rot | Powdery mildew | Nonliving spray residue
confirmation: Use culture and molecular identification for Sclerotinia confirmation. | Photograph infection site, internal stem/crown condition when available, and whole-plant distribution.
immediateActions: Isolate strongly affected plants and preserve diagnostic tissue before disposal.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Limit carryover of infected plant debris and conditions that keep susceptible tissue wet for extended periods.
warnings: White mold appearance is not specific to Sclerotinia. | The 2025 Cannabis pathogenicity report supports the organism as a real disease cause but not image-only species identification. | Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor should not be separated by canopy appearance alone; crown signs, sclerotia, culture, and molecular evidence carry more weight.

name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A lower- and inner-canopy hemp leaf-spot syndrome caused by Septoria species. Dark pycnidia within expanding brown-gray lesions are useful evidence, but modern work shows more than one Septoria species can infect Cannabis.
affectedParts: older lower leaves | inner canopy leaves | leaf lesions
stages: vegetative | flower | field production
indicators: Disease often begins on lower or inner-canopy leaves | Small irregular brown-to-gray spots expand to several millimeters | Dark round pycnidia can be visible within lesions | Older leaves may defoliate as disease advances
exclusions: Sooty conidial masses on the underside support Pseudocercospora | White-centered round lesions with a pronounced dark border support Cercospora as a differential | Shot-hole lesions and Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose | No fungal structures or lab evidence are present and an abiotic exposure fits the distribution better
lookAlikes: Cercospora leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Pseudocercospora olive leaf spot | Anthracnose

correctivePlan: Use confirmed-disease sanitation and environmental management appropriate to the system. | Track new lesion development after intervention.
prevention: Scout lower and inner canopy foliage early. | Reduce prolonged leaf wetness and carryover of infected debris where practical.
warnings: Septoria species taxonomy on Cannabis is not reducible to visual symptoms. | Do not train a species classifier from mixed Septoria figures without organism-confirmed labels.

name: Southern blight
summary: A warm-condition soilborne Cannabis disease centered at the soil line, crown and taproot. White cottony mycelium plus tan-to-brown spherical sclerotia at the plant base are strong signs, but wilt alone is nonspecific.
affectedParts: lower stem at soil line | crown | taproot | root surface | whole plant
stages: vegetative | reproductive | warm field conditions
indicators: Dark brown-to-tan discoloration develops near the soil line | Rot extends into crown or taproot while foliage yellows and the plant wilts/collapses | White cottony mycelium develops on basal tissue or adjacent soil | Numerous spherical tan-to-dark-brown sclerotia occur with compatible basal rot
exclusions: No basal rot, mycelium or sclerotia are present and measured drought explains wilt | Laboratory evidence identifies Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, Pythium or another root/crown pathogen | White growth is confined to leaves/flowers without basal disease
lookAlikes: Rhizoctonia root rot / sore shin | Fusarium crown/root rot | Pythium root rot | Sclerotinia white mold | Severe root-zone hypoxia
confirmation: Inspect the soil line/crown/root surface for characteristic mycelium and sclerotia and submit tissue/culture for organism confirmation. | Record temperature/moisture context, but do not use hot wet conditions as diagnostic proof.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone material and prevent movement of contaminated soil or debris to clean areas. | Preserve basal tissue and sclerotia for diagnostic testing.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed soilborne-disease sanitation and crop-legal management appropriate to the setting. | Address excess moisture where measured without assuming moisture correction eliminates established pathogen inoculum.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil or plant debris between production areas. | Monitor crown/root health during warm wet periods.
warnings: Whole-plant wilt alone cannot identify southern blight. | Sclerotia and laboratory evidence are substantially stronger than canopy appearance.

name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: individual leaflet sectors | entire leaflet portions | successive leaves from one shoot or meristem | one branch or clonal lineage | whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: vegetative | flowering; stage specificity is not established

lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause | Beet curly top virus disease | Hop latent viroid | Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus | Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder | Root-zone pH or EC disorder | Thrips, mites, or leafminer injury | Herbicide or plant-growth-regulator injury | Spray or high-light injury | Normal senescence or cultivar pigmentation | Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact

name: Armyworm caterpillar feeding complex
summary: A late-season caterpillar feeding differential for hemp. Armyworm larvae can defoliate foliage and enter buds or flowers, but species-level identification requires larval morphology rather than damage pattern alone.
