name: Cabbage looper feeding injury
summary: A chewing-caterpillar diagnosis that requires a Trichoplusia ni larva linked to fresh Cannabis injury. Irregular holes, windowpane feeding, frass, flowers with missing tissue, an adult moth, or a green looping caterpillar alone are not species-level ground truth.
affectedParts: abaxial and adaxial leaf surfaces | lower foliage reported in Missouri hemp | upper foliage if injury expands | leaf blade and interveinal tissue | floral buds and flower tissue reported in Missouri hemp
stages: vegetative foliage | flowering hemp | outdoor crop when larvae are present; calendar timing is regional
indicators: A pale-green, relatively smooth larva is physically linked to fresh chewing on the same Cannabis leaf or flower | The larva arches its body into a characteristic loop while crawling; behavior should be captured on video rather than inferred from one curved pose | A ventral macro view shows two pairs of abdominal prolegs on abdominal segments five and six, with the terminal anal pair recorded separately | Thin white longitudinal stripes occur along the back and sides, and the body narrows toward the anterior and broadens toward the posterior | Fresh lower-surface feeding or translucent windowpanes can precede through-leaf, irregular holes; this early-instar sequence is cross-crop transfer context unless recorded longitudinally on Cannabis | Sticky frass occurs beside a fresh feeding site and is linked to the photographed larva rather than treated as species-specific by itself | Missouri hemp guidance reports feeding beginning from lower-leaf undersides and moving upward, with severe injury capable of stripping foliage or damaging floral buds; other regions and cultivars may not follow this distribution | Detached Cannabis leaves support Trichoplusia ni feeding, but consumption and larval growth varied between the limited cannabinoid-free and CBD-dominant F2 genotypes tested
exclusions: No larva, specimen, fresh feeding front, or linked frass is found after repeat underside, canopy, and flower scouting; retain only a generic historical chewing-injury label | The larva has four pairs of abdominal prolegs or another complete proleg pattern inconsistent with cabbage looper | Dark thoracic legs or microscopic body microspines support soybean looper; unresolved plusiine larvae remain genus-, subfamily-, or caterpillar-level observations | A green caterpillar appears in a still image without a usable ventral proleg view, scale, looping-gait sequence, or expert specimen determination | Skeletonization is associated with aggregating metallic-green, copper-winged Japanese beetle adults rather than a caterpillar | Shot holes or ragged margins are linked to flea beetles or spotted cucumber beetles, or rasping holes and slime are linked to slugs or snails | Torn tissue aligns with hail, handling, fan abrasion, training damage, or spray injury and no chewing organism or fresh frass is linked to the lesion | An adult moth, egg, pupa, cocoon, frass deposit, or non-Cannabis larva is documented without a larva-linked Cannabis feeding event
lookAlikes: Soybean looper or another plusiine looper | Imported cabbageworm | Armyworm or fall armyworm | Corn earworm or tobacco budworm | Other green caterpillar or inchworm | Japanese beetle | Spotted cucumber beetle | Flea beetle feeding | Slug or snail feeding | Grasshopper feeding | Hail, wind, handling, or training tear | Spray or contact injury that later tears
confirmation: Capture whole-plant and row views and record affected and unaffected plants, upper/middle/lower canopy zones, leaf age, both leaf surfaces, and flower involvement; do not infer a universal lower-canopy preference from one Missouri guide or a detached-leaf assay. | At the fresh feeding front, record the larva and damage in the same uninterrupted sequence, then obtain dorsal, lateral, and ventral macro views with a millimeter scale. | Record video of the larva moving so the looping gait is observed, not reconstructed from a still pose; show two abdominal proleg pairs on segments five and six and retain the terminal anal pair in view. | Preserve a representative larva or rear it to an adult and seek Extension-entomologist or diagnostic-laboratory identification when soybean looper, another plusiine, or incomplete morphology remains plausible. | Mark plants and repeat counts and fixed-view imaging to separate expanding injury from old residual holes; log eggs, larvae, frass, cocoons, adults, and damaged area as separate observations. | Keep damage-only, frass-only, egg-only, adult-only, cocoon-only, non-Cannabis, detached-leaf-only, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, low-resolution, and organism/injury-unlinked samples out of the confirmed Trichoplusia ni Cannabis class. | Retain the Stack et al. detached-leaf assay as direct host-feeding evidence but flag it as a model-herbivore laboratory result: the study did not observe Trichoplusia ni in its field plots and does not supply a hemp action threshold, field distribution, or universal cultivar response.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and preserve the organism-to-damage link before moving, collecting, or treating the larva. | Inspect both surfaces of lower, middle, and upper leaves plus flowers; count larvae and map fresh versus old injury across several plants and locations. | Quarantine collected larvae with plant and location identifiers for expert review or rearing when species morphology is incomplete.
correctivePlan: Base any intervention on confirmed active larvae, observed injury trend, crop stage, local Extension advice, and products currently legal and labeled for hemp in the jurisdiction. | Do not apply Virginia cole-crop thresholds, laboratory chemotype effects, or non-Cannabis treatment results as hemp thresholds. | Revisit fixed plants after intervention because holes and missing flower tissue will not reverse and cannot alone demonstrate current control.
prevention: Include leaf-underside, whole-canopy, flower, larval dorsal/ventral/lateral macro, gait video, frass, and fixed-site progression views in routine scouting. | Record nearby crops and weeds, weather, crop stage, cultivar, and cannabinoid chemotype when known without assuming those variables predict infestation. | Conserve predators and parasitoids where compatible with local IPM guidance, while recording parasitized or diseased larvae separately from healthy active feeders.
warnings: Chewing morphology is shared by many insects and physical injuries; species-level ground truth requires a diagnostic larva linked to fresh Cannabis feeding. | Looping gait and a green striped body are not independently unique to Trichoplusia ni; soybean looper and other plusiines may require microscopic or expert determination. | The direct Cannabis study used Trichoplusia ni as a model generalist in detached-leaf assays and did not observe it in the field experiment; it cannot establish field prevalence, progression, distribution, yield loss, or thresholds. | Cannabinoid-free and CBD-dominant F2 genotypes differed in feeding and larval growth in one controlled study, but genotype, chemotype, and trichome context prevent a universal cultivar or severity rule. | Virginia and Florida timing, crop injury, generation, and management statements are non-Cannabis transfer evidence only; no validated hemp economic or treatment threshold was found. | The licensed University of Georgia organism image shows a non-Cannabis larva only. It is useful for morphology review but cannot label Cannabis injury, host use, severity, location, or progression and must remain outside Cannabis training and evaluation splits. | All damage-only, incomplete-morphology, detached-tissue, organism-only, non-Cannabis, unlinked, rights-unclear, and low-resolution samples require human review.

name: Dectes stem-borer injury
summary: A documented industrial-hemp stem-borer differential. Hemp evidence supports pith galleries, wilt, dieback, swollen or split stems, and breakage; species-level confidence requires a compatible larva or identified adult linked to the affected plant because those injury signs overlap disease, other borers, and mechanical failure.
affectedParts: leaf petiole as an early scouting location | main stem exterior | central pith and internal stem gallery | stem base and crown region | individual leaf or branch above the entry site | whole plant secondarily after structural failure
stages: outdoor vegetative hemp | outdoor flowering hemp | maturing field crop | post-harvest stem residue
indicators: A symptomatic hemp stem contains a longitudinal gallery through the central pith rather than only superficial bark injury | A legless cream to yellow larva with an orange-red head and accordion-like, rear-tapering body is recovered within the gallery | A dark-bodied adult covered by dense gray pubescence has very long, black-and-gray banded antennae and is linked to the affected plant or local infestation | One leaf or branch wilts or dies while surrounding canopy tissue remains initially greener, prompting inspection of its petiole and connected stem | The hemp stem is locally swollen, split, weakened, or broken and the internal gallery continues through the damaged region | Serial stem dissections show pith tunneling progressing toward lower stem tissue rather than a static wound cavity
exclusions: No internal pith gallery is present and wilt follows measured drought, waterlogging, heat, or root-zone failure | Vascular discoloration, crown lesions, root rot, or laboratory evidence supports Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, Pythium, or another vascular/root pathogen without a compatible larva | A clean fracture, training wound, wind split, or equipment injury has healthy intact pith on both sides and no tunnel, frass, or insect | The recovered larva has legs or morphology inconsistent with a cerambycid stem borer | The adult is an ashgray blister beetle or another gray beetle and lacks compatible longhorn morphology | A hollow or senescent stem is labeled from appearance alone without an active gallery, larva, adult association, or expert identification | Soybean-only basal girdling, frass-plug, field-edge, seasonal, or lodging patterns are transferred to hemp without Cannabis observations | Adult presence alone is used to infer that a photographed Cannabis stem is internally infested
lookAlikes: Fusarium stem or crown disease | Rhizoctonia crown or lower-stem rot | Pythium or other root-zone wilt | Mechanical training split or wind breakage | Drought or hydraulic wilt | Other stem-boring beetle or moth larva | Ashgray blister beetle adult | Normal mature hollow-stem or post-harvest decay
confirmation: Capture a whole-plant and row view before cutting, showing affected and unaffected plants and the precise canopy position of wilt or breakage. | Record a continuous video from the external symptom to the connected petiole or stem, then split the stem lengthwise on camera so the gallery-to-symptom relationship is preserved. | Photograph the intact stem exterior, entry or swelling site, cross-section, full longitudinal gallery, frass if present, and larva in situ with a metric scale and color reference. | Obtain dorsal, lateral, antenna, head-capsule, and full-body macro views of recovered adults or larvae; do not identify Dectes from a damaged stem alone. | Sample several symptomatic and asymptomatic stems across several field locations because one adult, one wilted leaf, or one gallery cannot establish field distribution. | Submit the organism and connected stem section to an Extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory when morphology is incomplete or another borer/blister beetle is plausible. | Pair insect confirmation with vascular and root-zone inspection when wilt, dieback, or crown decline could represent a co-occurring pathogen.
immediateActions: Flag affected plants and preserve the symptom-to-stem connection before pruning, disposal, or destructive sampling. | Quarantine removed stem material from clean production areas until the insect and any co-occurring disease are evaluated. | Map plants with fresh wilt, stem swelling, galleries, larvae, adults, and breakage as separate observations rather than one combined severity label.
correctivePlan: Base any response on confirmed Cannabis infestation, local Extension guidance, crop stage, and products or cultural practices currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction. | Remove or manage confirmed infested residues only when compatible with local agronomic, sanitation, erosion, and regulatory requirements. | Continue fixed-plant monitoring after intervention because existing galleries, wilted leaves, and broken stems will not reverse and cannot alone measure current control.
prevention: Add stem exterior, petiole, split-stem, larva/adult macro, and whole-row views to routine outdoor scouting records. | Record adjacent soybean, sunflower, ragweed, and cocklebur context as potential regional reservoirs without assuming those host relationships predict Cannabis infestation. | Retain specimens and source-grouped sequences so future expert review can keep plants, stems, organisms, dates, and field locations together.
warnings: Wilt, dieback, swollen stems, splits, galleries, and breakage are not independently species-specific; Dectes ground truth requires organism evidence linked to the affected hemp stem. | Published Cannabis evidence is currently much thinner than soybean and sunflower evidence. Non-Cannabis leaf-age, canopy, seasonal, girdling, lodging, yield, and management claims are transfer context only. | An organism-only adult image teaches morphology but cannot establish Cannabis host use, an internal larva, active injury, severity, or field distribution. | The Dectes texanus versus historical Dectes sayi boundary includes ambiguous morphology; incomplete adult views require expert or molecular review rather than a forced species label. | Adult counts do not reliably predict infested-stem frequency in soybean and no validated hemp action threshold or symptom-to-yield relationship was found. | The institutional video is soybean-focused and has no verified reusable license; it is reference metadata only and must not enter Cannabis training or evaluation splits. | All damage-only, gallery-only, organism-only, unlinked specimen/stem, non-Cannabis, and unresolved-taxonomy samples require human review.

name: Japanese beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented outdoor-hemp defoliator and flower feeder. Fresh skeletonization plus an adult with metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve white abdominal hair patches is strong field evidence; feeding damage without the adult is only a low-specificity chewing-injury label.
affectedParts: upper and lower leaf surfaces | interveinal leaf blade | major and minor veins left after feeding | developing flowers | tender shoots
stages: vegetative outdoor hemp | developing flower | late-season outdoor crop
indicators: Adults on hemp have a metallic-green head and thorax with copper-bronze wing covers | Five white hair patches along each abdominal side plus two posterior patches form twelve visible tufts when the adult is photographed from above and slightly behind | Fresh chewing removes interveinal leaf tissue while leaving a lace-like network of veins | Adults are present on the same leaf, shoot, or developing flower as fresh feeding injury | Multiple adults and newly expanding damage occur in a localized plant or field cluster | Flower feeding is directly observed rather than inferred from missing or browned floral tissue
exclusions: No adult or specimen is recovered after repeat scouting and another defoliator is found at the fresh feeding front | The beetle lacks the twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches or morphology supports green June beetle, another scarab, or a metallic beetle | Holes contain caterpillars, silk, or frass and do not preserve the characteristic interveinal lace pattern | Small round shot holes with flea beetles support flea-beetle injury | Irregular holes or ragged margins occur with spotted cucumber beetles rather than Japanese beetles | Damage is mined within intact epidermis rather than removed from the leaf surface | Skeletonization is old, dry, and unchanged across serial observations, with no active organism established | Root decline is attributed to Japanese beetle solely because adults occur above ground; hemp-root grub feeding has not been confirmed
lookAlikes: Green June beetle or another scarab beetle | Spotted cucumber beetle | Flea beetle feeding | Cabbage looper | Armyworm or another caterpillar | Grasshopper feeding | Leafminer injury | Hail or mechanical tearing
confirmation: Capture a whole-plant or row view to show the distribution of affected and unaffected plants, then record upper, middle, and lower canopy zones separately; published hemp sources do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position. | Photograph fresh injury and the adult together before disturbance, then obtain dorsal, lateral, and posterior macro views with a scale reference. | Verify the metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches; preserve a representative adult when morphology is unclear. | Revisit marked leaves or plants and record new feeding and adult counts so old residual skeletonization is separated from an active infestation. | For image/video datasets, require an organism-level frame linked to the damage sequence; do not use skeletonization-only frames as species-level ground truth. | Submit an intact adult to an Extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory when a similar scarab, green June beetle, or incomplete view prevents confident identification. | Do not infer larval root injury from adult canopy presence; confirm grubs in the root zone and identify them separately if root damage is suspected.
immediateActions: Mark sampled plants, count adults, estimate current defoliation, and record whether flowers are being fed on before choosing an intervention. | Scout several plants across several locations so one conspicuous aggregation is not treated as a field-wide population estimate. | Preserve pre-intervention photographs and a representative specimen when the diagnosis or future label review depends on species identity.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed adults, fresh injury, crop stage, local pressure, and products currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction. | Track new injury and adult counts at fixed plants; old skeletonized tissue will not recover and should not be used alone to judge control. | Protect pollinators and flowering-crop quality when evaluating any response on developing flowers.
prevention: Include adult-morphology and fresh-damage views in routine outdoor scouting records. | Map clusters and repeat counts through the adult activity period instead of relying on cumulative season-long damage. | Treat pheromone traps as monitoring tools only after evaluating placement; attraction near the crop can confound local abundance and damage.
warnings: Skeletonization, irregular holes, or flower injury alone are not Japanese beetle ground truth; species-level image labels require the adult and diagnostic morphology. | A close-up adult specimen image can teach organism morphology but cannot establish Cannabis host association, active feeding, severity, canopy distribution, or yield impact. | Published hemp observations do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position, so those fields must be recorded from the sampled plant rather than imputed. | The 2019 multi-state synthesis called Japanese beetle potentially significant but also reported serious defoliation as rare across the broader defoliator complex; apparent severity must remain case-specific. | No universal hemp economic threshold, symptom-to-yield conversion, or cultivar response is established by these sources. | The UNH hemp photograph is institutional and creator-credited but has no explicit reuse license on its landing page; store only its reference metadata unless permission is obtained. | All damage-only, incomplete-morphology, unlinked specimen/damage, and root-injury samples require human review.

name: Spotted cucumber beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented industrial-hemp chewing pest. Adult beetles can damage foliage and floral tissue while larvae can injure root hairs and root tips; organism evidence is needed because ragged holes and weak roots are not species-specific.
affectedParts: leaves | leaf margins | flowers | pollen-bearing tissue | root hairs | root tips
stages: vegetative | early flower | field production
indicators: Yellow-green adult beetles with twelve dark spots are present on hemp | Leaves or floral tissue show fresh holes and ragged chewing edges while adults are feeding | Root injury or weak anchorage occurs together with compatible rootworm larvae in the root zone
exclusions: No compatible beetles or larvae are found and another chewing pest is present | Damage consists mainly of stippling, silvering, mining, or sap-feeding distortion rather than chewing | Root decline occurs without root-feeding larvae and a pathogen or irrigation disorder is better supported
lookAlikes: Japanese beetle | Armyworm / caterpillar feeding | Cabbage looper | Mechanical tearing | Root disease
confirmation: Photograph or collect the beetle/larva with the damaged tissue; identify the organism rather than assigning species from holes alone. | Inspect roots only when root symptoms or lodging are present.
immediateActions: Scout nearby plants for adults and fresh feeding damage. | Document root-zone larvae separately from above-ground beetles.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response appropriate to confirmed pest pressure, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout field margins and foliage during vegetative to early flowering growth. | Reduce weed or alternate-host reservoirs where agronomically appropriate.
warnings: Chewing holes are not diagnostic of spotted cucumber beetle. | Root damage can coexist with root pathogens; finding beetle larvae does not exclude disease.

name: Tarnished plant bug occurrence and possible feeding injury
scientificName: Lygus lineolaris and other Lygus spp.
summary: Lygus adults and nymphs are documented residents of field hemp and can breed on the crop, but organism presence is not proof that a photographed symptom was caused by tarnished plant bug. Earlier peer-reviewed hemp observations and current Utah guidance report no documented foliar symptoms, while Missouri Extension lists chlorotic spotting and terminal or bud distortion. Treat foliar and reproductive injury as compatible, contested evidence until a correctly identified insect is repeatedly linked to fresh injury; hemp economic thresholds remain unestablished.
affectedParts: whole plant and canopy for organism scouting | upper and expanding foliage as a contested symptom location | shoot tips and terminals as a contested symptom location | flowers and inflorescences for adult and nymph scouting | developing seeds and seed heads in seed hemp | nearby weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, and field-edge vegetation as possible source habitat
stages: field emergence through harvest | vegetative field hemp | flowering field hemp | seed development | regional summer scouting window
indicators: A captured adult is 4.4 to 6.3 mm long, light green to mottled brown or black, and has a V-shaped or triangular mark on the scutellum; the mark supports genus-level screening but is not sufficient for Lygus lineolaris identification | A compatible nymph is green or yellow-green, wingless or developing wing pads, rounded, and marked by dark dorsal spots; direct macro views must separate it from aphids and beneficial big-eyed bugs | Adults and multiple nymph sizes are recovered repeatedly from the same hemp area by direct inspection, sweep net, beating tray, or vacuum sampling, supporting residency or breeding rather than a transient single-insect observation | Counts are mapped across field edge and interior, upper and lower canopy, nearby alternate hosts, crop stage, and date because Lygus distribution can reflect colonization from weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, or other hosts | Shriveled or deformed developing seed, flower or bud loss, and abortion are compatible reproductive-tissue observations only when fresh injury is linked to feeding insects; appearance alone does not establish Lygus causation | Chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, and distorted buds are low-specificity, source-conflicted hemp observations: Missouri Extension lists them, whereas the 2019 peer-reviewed synthesis and Utah Extension state that foliar symptoms had not been documented | In Pacific Northwest context only, counts may rise from late July to mid-August near flowering; calendar timing must not be transferred to other regions, environments, or cultivars as a diagnostic feature
exclusions: Repeated sweep, beating-tray, vacuum, flower, and direct visual sampling finds no compatible adults or nymphs while symptoms continue to progress | The insect is Lygus hesperus, Lygus elisus, another mirid, or remains genus-only; do not assign Lygus lineolaris from a pale triangular mark alone | A beneficial big-eyed bug, false chinch bug, stink bug, aphid, or another seed or plant bug better matches the captured organism | Aphids with cornicles and colonies, honeydew, or cast skins explain the observation rather than fast-moving Lygus nymphs | Magnification confirms broad mite or hemp russet mite populations on the distorted tissue | Chewing holes, frass, silk, mines, galleries, or recovered larvae support a caterpillar, beetle, leafminer, or borer instead of piercing-sucking injury | A spray, herbicide, heat, wind, hail, training, or mechanical exposure pattern explains the distortion without organism-linked fresh injury | Boron or another nutrient/root-zone disorder is supported by measured inputs, root-zone pH or EC, tissue analysis, and a distribution pattern independent of Lygus counts | Flower or seed injury is assigned from one late-season frame without paired healthy tissue, repeated insect counts, crop-use context, or exclusion of pollination, pathogen, and abiotic causes
lookAlikes: Western tarnished plant bug (Lygus hesperus) | Pale legume bug (Lygus elisus) | Big-eyed bug (Geocoris spp., beneficial predator) | False chinch bug or another seed bug | Stink bug nymph or adult | Aphid nymph or cannabis aphid colony | Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Thrips feeding injury | Boron deficiency or another root-zone nutrient disorder | Herbicide, spray, heat, hail, wind, training, or mechanical injury | Pollination, flower pathogen, or normal seed-development variation
confirmation: Record a linked capture set: whole plant, upper/middle/lower canopy, terminal or flower/seed-head context, dorsal and lateral insect macro views, a size scale, and a short video showing movement and the exact plant part occupied. | Sample multiple symptomatic and asymptomatic plants across field edge and interior on at least two dates using the same sweep-net, beating-tray, vacuum, or timed-inspection method; retain counts by adult and nymph stage. | Identify a captured adult or diagnostic later instar with an entomologist or validated regional key. Keep triangular-mark-only, low-resolution, nymph-only, and genus-only observations out of the Lygus lineolaris confirmed class. | Link the identified organism to fresh injury on the same plant and tissue over time. A specimen from an unrelated weed, trap, plant, date, or field supports local occurrence but not Cannabis causation. | For reproductive injury, compare affected and unaffected flowers or seeds from the same cultivar and stage, document pollination and crop-use context, and exclude pathogens, caterpillars, stink bugs, nutrition, and abiotic injury. | For foliar or terminal symptoms, retain a source-conflict flag and cap image/video-only confidence at 0.30 because authoritative hemp sources disagree and two sources report no documented foliage symptoms. | Keep symptom-only, insect-only, detached-tissue-only, stock, vendor, generated, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of automated training and confirmed ground truth.
immediateActions: Pause species-specific treatment decisions while collecting repeatable organism and injury evidence; isolate the label from other distorted-growth records. | Scout flowers, terminals, whole plants, nearby weeds, and field margins with a documented method, while preserving representative adults or nymphs for identification. | Record cultivar, crop use, plant sex, flowering or seed stage, location, date, weather, recent sprays, root-zone measurements, and other organisms before interpreting injury.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated pest-management response only after local identification, repeated population assessment, and plant-linked injury justify action; follow current hemp labels and local regulations. | Do not use an unvalidated numeric threshold or transfer seed-crop, regional, or non-Cannabis injury assumptions to cannabinoid, fiber, indoor, or other production systems.
prevention: Maintain a repeatable field-edge and interior scouting record from emergence through harvest, with added flower and seed-head sampling when those tissues develop. | Track nearby weeds, alfalfa, quinoa, and other possible source hosts without removing flowering vegetation impulsively; account for beneficial insects and local habitat-management guidance. | Retain paired healthy and affected captures so future review can distinguish occurrence, breeding, active feeding, and confirmed injury.
warnings: Lygus presence on hemp is documented, but presence alone does not prove that a visible Cannabis symptom was caused by tarnished plant bug. | Authoritative hemp sources conflict on foliar injury: Missouri Extension lists spotting, curling, stunting, and distortion, while the 2019 peer-reviewed synthesis and Utah Extension report no documented foliage symptoms. | A pale V-shaped or triangular scutellar mark is shared across Lygus species and cannot establish Lygus lineolaris without an adequate specimen and expert or key-based identification. | No validated hemp economic or treatment threshold is available, and reproductive injury significance varies with seed, fiber, and cannabinoid production context. | The public-domain USDA image is an organism-only laboratory nymph reference on a non-Cannabis plant; it is not Cannabis damage ground truth and is excluded from automated training. | No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis Lygus injury image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch.

name: Thrips feeding injury
summary: Onion thrips and western flower thrips are documented on hemp; feeding can produce vein-associated white flecks or irregular silvery scars, dark fecal spots, and distortion of leaves damaged while expanding, but symptoms alone cannot identify the insect or its species.
affectedParts: leaf upper and lower surfaces | leaf veins and adjacent lamina | young expanding leaves | growing tips | flowers and pollen-bearing tissue
stages: propagation | vegetative | pre-flower | flower
indicators: Irregular white flecks or silvery scarred patches, often following or crossing veins | Small dark fecal spots occur within or beside fresh feeding scars | Minute elongated yellow, tan, or yellow-brown insects are recovered from symptomatic tissue | Wingless creamy-yellow larvae or slender adults with narrow fringed wings are visible under magnification | Leaves fed on while developing later expand with localized distortion or uneven scarred areas | Indoor or protected-crop injury increases over serial observations while matched uninfested plants remain unchanged
exclusions: No thrips, larvae, shed skins, or dark fecal spots are found after repeat inspection, foliage tapping, and sticky-card monitoring | Fine webbing, round eggs, and two-spotted mites are present | Microscopic cigar-shaped mites with two pairs of legs are present | Only residue is visible and it wipes or dissolves without damaged epidermal tissue beneath it | The pattern follows a nutrient-mobility gradient by leaf age rather than localized feeding scars | Circular or angular lesions enlarge independently and have halos, fungal growth, bacterial streaming, or pathogen-positive laboratory results | Distortion is restricted to the newest protected tissue and broad mites or dotted broad-mite eggs are confirmed | Abrasion aligns uniformly with a fan, rubbing surface, spray event, or physical contact and no organisms are recovered
lookAlikes: Two-spotted spider mites | Hemp russet mite | Broad mite | Foliar spray or mineral residue | Wind or contact abrasion | Edema or physiological corking | Nutrient or root-zone disorder | Leaf-spot pathogen | Beneficial predatory thrips
confirmation: Inspect both leaf surfaces, veins, folds, growing tips, and flowers with at least a 10× hand lens; record whether scars, dark fecal spots, larvae, adults, and shed skins occur together. | Tap symptomatic foliage and flowers over white paper or a collection tray, then preserve representative insects for magnified examination. | Use blue or yellow sticky cards as population and movement monitors, not as proof that a particular damaged leaf was caused by thrips. | For species-level labels, submit intact adults to an entomology or plant diagnostic laboratory for morphological or validated molecular identification; color and a routine phone photograph are insufficient. | Capture serial whole-plant, leaf-surface macro, opposite-surface, vein-level, and organism-magnification views with scale and production context; compare with a matched healthy plant.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly mark suspect plants and inspect neighboring propagation material, young growth, flowers, weeds, and sticky cards before moving plants. | Preserve representative insects and pre-treatment images before intervention when species or causal confirmation is needed. | Avoid applying an unverified pesticide or coating simply because silver injury is present.
correctivePlan: Use only a control program legal for Cannabis or hemp, the jurisdiction, production system, and growth stage, following the current product label and worker-safety requirements. | Track fresh scars and organism counts at fixed sampling sites; old silver scars and distorted leaves will not heal and should not be used alone to judge control. | Address confirmed entry or reservoir points such as infested transplants, weeds, crop debris, flowers, or unscreened openings while conserving identified beneficial thrips and other natural enemies.
prevention: Quarantine and hand-lens inspect incoming clones and transplants. | Scout representative plants and canopy zones on a fixed schedule, including young leaves and flowers rather than relying only on sticky cards. | Maintain clean plant and weed-free buffer practices appropriate to the production system and record thrips detections by stage and location.
warnings: Silver flecks, black specks, or distorted leaves alone are not thrips ground truth; confirm the organism and feeding context. | A group-level thrips label does not establish onion thrips, western flower thrips, tobacco thrips, or another species; species identification requires suitable adult specimens and specialist examination. | The controlled yield study was preliminary and used defined indoor infestation treatments; it does not establish a universal economic threshold or symptom-to-yield conversion. | Predatory thrips can be beneficial, so the presence of a thrips-shaped insect is not sufficient to assign a damaging-pest label. | The two institutional Cannabis images below have no explicit reuse license; they are hidden metadata references, not copied assets or training samples.

name: Broad mite
summary: A microscopic tarsonemid mite that hides in protected young tissue; feeding injury appears later as hardened, puckered, cupped, or strap-like new leaves, bronzing, short internodes, and deformed buds.
affectedParts: youngest expanding leaves | leaf undersides | leaf axils | growing tips | flower buds | shaded or protected canopy tissue
stages: propagation | vegetative | pre-flower | flower
indicators: Warped, puckered, or hardened newest leaves | Cupped or strap-like new growth | Bronze, copper, or dark discoloration on young tissue | Short internodes and stunted growing tips | Deformed or aborted flower buds | Oval mites or dotted translucent eggs under magnification
exclusions: Cigar-shaped mites with only two pairs of legs are present instead | Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present | Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient symptom pattern | Injury is uniform on the brightest upper canopy and measured leaf temperature or light is excessive | No mites or dotted eggs are found after repeat sampling of adjacent fresh growth and protected sites
lookAlikes: Hemp russet mite | Cyclamen mite | Heat or light stress | Plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury | Micronutrient or root-zone disorder | Virus-like or developmental distortion
confirmation: Inspect fresh expanding tissue adjacent to the worst damage, including undersides, axils, growing tips, and buds, at about 20× or with a dissecting microscope. | Confirm translucent oval adults and clear oval eggs bearing raised pale dots; adult females may show a pale dorsal stripe. | Separate broad mite from cigar-shaped, two-pair-legged russet mites and from cyclamen mites, whose eggs lack the characteristic dotted surface. | Treat a negative sample cautiously because injury can persist after mites leave badly damaged tissue; repeat sampling across plants and time when suspicion remains.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings or shared tools into clean areas. | Microscope-screen neighboring plants before choosing any control.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current label. | Track mites or eggs on fixed fresh-growth sampling sites; do not judge response from old distorted leaves. | Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and sanitize shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected propagation material. | Quarantine and magnification-screen incoming clones. | Include protected new-growth sites in routine scouting rather than inspecting only mature fan leaves.
warnings: Leaf distortion, bronzing, or short internodes alone are not diagnostic. | The two media assets below show the organism without a host and are morphology references, not cannabis symptom ground truth. | Although their licenses permit reuse, both remain reference-only and excluded from automated training pending a separate training and dataset-split review.

name: Hemp russet mite
summary: A microscopic eriophyid mite whose feeding can cause localized bronzing, brittle or reduced leaves, distorted edges, stunting, and suppressed floral growth without the webbing typical of spider mites.
affectedParts: young leaves | leaf undersides | petioles | stems | growing tips | flower buds
stages: vegetative | pre-flower | flower
indicators: Dull gray or bronzed foliage | Brittle or reduced leaf size | Leaf edges curl upward or downward | Stem or petiole bronzing | Stunted growing tips | No webbing despite mite-like damage
exclusions: Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present | Only interveinal chlorosis follows an older-leaf nutrient pattern | Damage is restricted to the hottest or brightest canopy surface | No cigar-shaped mites are found after adequate microscope sampling
lookAlikes: Two-spotted spider mites | Thrips | Broad mites | Heat or light stress | Nutrient or root-zone stress | Powdery residue
confirmation: Sample both symptomatic and adjacent apparently healthy leaves; inspect undersides, midribs, petioles, and protected trichome zones with a dissecting or digital microscope. | Confirm pale, cigar-shaped eriophyid mites with only two pairs of legs; ordinary phone or whole-plant images are not sufficient. | For repeatable image counts, photograph multiple leaflet sections under microscope magnification rather than relying on a single field of view.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings, tools, clothing, or plant debris into clean areas. | Inspect nearby plants under adequate magnification before choosing a treatment.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current product label. | Track mite counts on fixed leaf positions after intervention; visible injury can lag behind population change. | Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and clean shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected, mite-free propagation material. | Quarantine and microscope-screen incoming clones. | Maintain routine microscope scouting because low populations can be visually silent.
warnings: Leaf curl or bronzing alone is not diagnostic. | Do not confuse tan cast-skin accumulations with fungal powder. | CC BY 4.0 permits reuse with attribution, but these hashed reference images remain excluded from model training until a separate training and dataset-split review is completed.

name: Two-spotted spider mites
summary: Twospotted spider mites feed mainly from leaf undersides, producing upper-surface stippling that can progress to chlorosis, necrosis, leaf loss, and silk webbing. Injury alone is nonspecific and can persist after mites leave, so an active label requires direct organism evidence.
affectedParts: lower leaf surface | upper leaf surface | canopy | flower
stages: all | vegetative | flower
indicators: Paired-leaf view: fine pale stippling or speckling on the upper surface corresponds to a colony, eggs, cast skins, or debris on the lower surface. | Adults are tiny, oval, pale yellowish to greenish mites whose two dark body spots may be visible in a sharp macro view; round translucent eggs occur near veins and webbing below the leaf. | Damage can expand from localized stippled leaves to bronze or yellow tissue, dry brown margins or whole leaves, premature leaf drop, and reduced vigor or flower growth. | Fine silk first appears in protected leaf regions and can bridge leaves, stems, or flowers when populations are high; visible webbing generally indicates an established infestation. | Hot, dry, dusty, or water-stressed zones can develop faster or denser hotspots, including field edges near dusty paths, but this spatial association is contextual evidence only.
exclusions: Silvery scraped streaks with black fecal specks and slender insects support thrips rather than spider mites. | Distorted newest growth with no webbing and mites too small for a hand lens supports hemp russet or broad-mite triage, not a two-spotted spider-mite label. | Fast-moving, long-legged, pear-shaped mites may be beneficial predators; do not label every visible mite as Tetranychus urticae. | Spray or mineral residue may wipe away and lacks eggs, moving life stages, cast skins, and silk anchored to the leaf. | Nutrient, root-zone, or water stress can produce chlorosis or necrosis but should not produce a matched underside colony or mite webbing. | Leafhopper injury can cause pale stippling without an underside mite colony; inspect for hoppers and the distribution of feeding marks.
lookAlikes: Thrips | Hemp russet mites | Broad mite injury | Predatory mites | Leafhopper feeding | Spray or mineral residue | Nutrient or root-zone stress
confirmation: Do not confirm an active infestation or species from stippling, chlorosis, or webbing in an image or video alone; capture the whole-canopy distribution plus paired upper- and lower-leaf views. | Inspect several symptomatic and adjacent apparently healthy leaf undersides with at least 10x magnification; record eggs, larvae or nymphs, adults, cast skins, fecal debris, and silk with a scale reference. | Tap suspect leaves or stems over clean white paper and record close video of moving organisms; distinguish slow plant-feeding mites from faster, longer-legged predatory mites. | For species-level ground truth, retain a specimen and obtain qualified entomologist or diagnostic-laboratory identification when morphology is not resolved by the capture. | Record cultivar, growth stage, canopy position, site or room, first-observed date, repeat counts from fixed leaves, temperature, humidity, dust, and water-stress context.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly flag affected plants and inspect neighboring plants before moving people, tools, or plant material through the area. | Preserve representative leaves or specimens for confirmation and record the pre-intervention organism count and visual distribution.
correctivePlan: Use a legal, crop- and stage-appropriate integrated pest-management plan selected for the production system; protect beneficial predators and follow all label restrictions. | Reinspect the same marked leaves and nearby plants at fixed intervals; use live-organism counts rather than persistent old stippling to judge whether the active population changed. | Reduce avoidable dust and water stress and examine weeds or adjacent host plants where relevant, while treating these as risk factors rather than diagnostic proof.
prevention: Quarantine and inspect incoming plants, especially leaf undersides, before they enter production. | Scout fixed leaves across canopy zones and field edges consistently, documenting both direct organisms and injury over time.
warnings: The published 0-to-5 visual scale came from one evaluator, two hemp cultivars, naturally occurring background mite populations, and flowering plants; it is an observational study reference, not a universal severity or treatment threshold. | No research-based action threshold has been established for North Carolina hemp across fiber, seed, and cannabinoid markets. | Injury-only imagery is not species-level ground truth: stippling is nonspecific, webbing is usually a later sign, and old injury can remain after mites have left. | Cultivar, canopy, environment, and production system can alter visible severity, and predatory mites or other pest mites can be confused with Tetranychus urticae in low-resolution media. | The linked CC BY 4.0 damage-scale figure is a mixed-grade composite; it remains training-ineligible and its panels are not independent samples without crop geometry, source-group, and label review. | Avoid applying any product unless it is legal for the crop, site, growth stage, and jurisdiction, especially on flowers.

name: Root-knot nematodes
summary: A Cannabis root-parasitic nematode complex in which small, firm, whitish root galls are the strongest visible cue. Gall morphology can support a root-knot differential, but species, race, burden, and causality require plant-linked root/soil nematode evidence because canopy effects and cultivar responses are nonspecific.
affectedParts: fine and lateral roots | complete root system | root galls and feeding sites | surrounding root-zone soil | whole plant secondarily
stages: post-establishment | vegetative | flower | field or container production
indicators: Small, firm, whitish localized galls are integrated into Cannabis root tissue; M. hapla, M. incognita, and M. javanica galls are often no more than about 4 mm | An intact washed root system shows the distribution and burden of true galls rather than an isolated swelling | Adult females within roots, associated egg masses, extracted juveniles, or quantified eggs accompany compatible galling | Root systems may show reduced development, lateral-root growth, or root weight as burden increases | Above-ground growth may become stunted or chlorotic, but no consistent leaf-age or canopy-position pattern is established | Morphology plus validated species-specific PCR or sequence evidence identifies Meloidogyne when a species-level label is required
exclusions: Root swellings are normal lateral-root branch points or other root anatomy rather than firm integrated galls | Circling, matted roots and container-wall geometry support root binding without plant-linked nematode recovery | Soft, water-soaked or sloughed roots plus oomycete evidence support Pythium or another water mold | Necrotic root or crown lesions plus fungal isolation or molecular evidence support Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, or another root pathogen | No galls or nematodes are found and measured drought, hypoxia, salinity, pH, or nutrient conditions explain the canopy response | Only canopy stunting, yellowing, wilt, or low vigor is visible without an intact root-system inspection | A detached or cropped gall close-up cannot be linked to the sampled Cannabis plant and surrounding soil | Root-knot species or race is inferred from gall size, color, cultivar response, or geography without organism-level testing
lookAlikes: Normal lateral-root branch points or root primordia | Root binding / circling roots | Pythium or other oomycete root rot | Rhizoctonia root rot / sore shin | Fusarium root or crown disease | Root-zone hypoxia / overwatering | Drought / water-deficit stress | High EC / fertilizer salt injury | Root-zone pH-driven nutrient unavailability | Nitrogen or other nutrient deficiency
confirmation: Capture the same plant at whole-canopy scale, then recover and gently wash the complete root system; photograph the intact root architecture and gall distribution with a scale before making close-ups or sections. | Collect representative galled roots and surrounding soil under the same plant identifier; keep canopy, root, soil, date, cultivar, substrate, and treatment metadata linked. | Extract and quantify juveniles or eggs from a defined soil volume and females or egg masses per defined root mass; absence from one cropped close-up does not establish absence from the root system. | Use adult-female and juvenile morphology together with a validated species-specific PCR or sequence assay when assigning a Meloidogyne species; gall appearance alone supports at most a root-knot complex label. | For high-confidence causal ground truth, require a plant-linked diagnostic result and compatible root signs; controlled pathogenicity or a documented reproduction factor is stronger than field association alone. | Record cultivar, nematode species or isolate, inoculum or starting population where known, sampling interval, and root-washing method because all can change visible burden and reproduction. | Keep canopy-only, symptom-only, detached-root-only, unlinked soil/root assay, species-from-gall, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed root-knot class.
immediateActions: Quarantine the sampled root-zone material and prevent movement of potentially infested soil, roots, runoff, tools, or containers into clean production areas. | Preserve representative galled roots and paired surrounding soil for nematode analysis before destructive treatment or disposal. | Measure root-zone moisture, pH, and EC and inspect for root binding and rot concurrently so a coincident abiotic or pathogen problem is not missed.
correctivePlan: Base any intervention on confirmed nematode identity, burden, crop stage, production system, and locally legal options; this record does not convert laboratory hemp-seed-extract assays into field treatment guidance. | Track response with repeated plant-linked canopy, root, and nematode-count observations rather than assuming visual recovery proves eradication.
prevention: Use clean planting material and media and avoid moving infested soil or root debris on tools, footwear, containers, or equipment. | When unexplained patches of poor growth occur, compare complete root systems and paired soil samples from affected and nearby apparently healthy plants. | Retain cultivar and source-lot metadata because susceptibility and reproduction vary materially among hemp cultivars and Meloidogyne species or isolates.
warnings: Above-ground chlorosis, wilt, and stunting are nonspecific and should receive very low diagnostic weight without linked root and organism evidence. | Small white hard galls support a root-knot differential but do not identify species or race; M. enterolobii can also produce larger galls. | Cultivar, Meloidogyne species or isolate, inoculum, pot size, and observation interval can alter gall burden, reproduction, and growth effects, so one image cannot define universal severity. | The Alabama field evidence was region-, cultivar-, and race-specific; do not generalize M. incognita Race 3 to every Cannabis root-knot case. | The 2025 article figures plot seed-extract bioassays rather than infected-root symptoms and are not diagnostic image ground truth. | Cannabis yield-loss thresholds and clean, cultivar-diverse, laboratory-linked image or video sequences remain incomplete.

name: Late-cycle leaf aging / senescence context
summary: Cannabis and hemp leaves can lose chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity as foliage ages and flowering advances, with stronger age and canopy-position effects in older or lower leaves; visible yellowing is neither required nor sufficient to classify the change as normal senescence.
affectedParts: physiologically older fan leaves | lower-canopy fan leaves | upper-canopy fan leaves assessed separately | whole canopy only as a mapped age gradient | inflorescences and sugar leaves as exclusion-check tissue
stages: flowering time series; strongest Cannabis evidence compares weeks 1, 5, and 9 after transition to a 12-hour photoperiod
indicators: Change is gradual across serial observations rather than abrupt between captures | Older or lower-position fan leaves change before recently expanded upper-canopy leaves | Chlorophyll index or photosynthetic capacity declines with documented leaf age even when a leaf remains visibly green | The same cultivar and production cohort shows a repeatable late-cycle age and canopy-position gradient | Inflorescences, recently expanded leaves, stems, and roots lack independent evidence of a spreading disorder | Color assessment is made under calibrated or repeatable lighting with healthy same-cultivar references
exclusions: Visible yellowing alone is used as proof of senescence or harvest readiness | Recently expanded or upper-canopy leaves decline first or as strongly as older lower leaves without an established age gradient | Chlorosis begins early, progresses rapidly, reduces whole-plant vigor, or spreads independently of leaf age | Interveinal chlorosis, marginal scorch, discrete lesions, rings, mosaic, distortion, brittle growth, webbing, feeding scars, frass, or visible organisms are present | Root-zone pH, EC, water content, oxygenation, root appearance, or irrigation history is abnormal | Feed composition, tissue or solution analysis, or response to correction supports nitrogen or another nutrient disorder | Inflorescence mold, necrosis, odor, collapse, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen | A lamp, spray, heat, cold, drought, salinity, or other exposure gradient explains the distribution better
lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or under-supply during flowering | Magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, or micronutrient disorder | Root-zone pH or EC disorder | Water shortage or excessive vapor demand | Overwatering or root hypoxia | Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease | Hop latent viroid | Beet curly top virus or unresolved systemic mosaic syndrome | Powdery mildew, Botrytis, or leaf-spot disease | Hemp russet mite, broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury | High-light, heat, cold, spray, or plant-growth-regulator injury | Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not label “normal fade,” senescence, ripeness, harvest readiness, nutrient depletion, or plant health from color in one photograph or video. | Record leaf node, leaf age, upper versus lower canopy, cultivar, flowering day, photoperiod, PPFD, temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, irrigation, and serial rate of change. | Capture whole-plant, canopy, branch, upper-leaf-surface, lower-leaf-surface, root-zone, and inflorescence views under repeatable lighting with a color reference and scale. | Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content or container weight, and inspect roots; review feed composition and, when consequential, use calibrated solution or tissue analysis rather than assuming remobilization. | Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification for mites, thrips, webbing, eggs, cast skins, frass, and feeding scars. | Use a plant diagnostic laboratory when lesions, systemic distortion, vascular or root decline, inflorescence disease, or virus/viroid signs remain plausible. | Compare several healthy same-cultivar plants from the same propagation cohort; an age-position gradient that repeats across serial observations is contextual support, not causal proof.
immediateActions: Keep the sample labeled “late-cycle leaf aging—cause unresolved” until exclusion checks are complete. | Preserve serial images and measured root-zone, environment, and nutrition records before changing the program. | Isolate or pause propagation from plants with systemic, pest, pathogen, or viroid warning signs.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured nutrient, pH, EC, irrigation, environment, pest, or pathogen problems; do not force yellowing or apply nitrogen solely from camera color. | Reassess recently expanded leaves, roots, and inflorescences after any evidence-based correction while recognizing that old yellow or necrotic tissue will not become a clean health indicator. | Retain the normal-development label only when progression remains slow, age-positioned, cultivar-consistent, and unsupported by competing diagnoses.
prevention: Maintain same-cultivar flowering timelines with leaf-node and canopy-position annotations. | Keep calibrated pH and EC records, irrigation history, environmental logs, pest scouting, and laboratory results linked to image and video samples. | Create healthy reference captures under fixed lighting and camera settings rather than relying on internet photographs or a universal week-of-flower chart.
warnings: A hemp leaf-aging study found photosynthetic capacity could decline while leaves remained green, so visible yellowing is not required for senescence. | The Stillwater flowering study found temporal and canopy-position changes but did not resolve how much was caused by leaf age versus whole-plant ontogeny and did not validate a universal visible fade. | Flowering Cannabis still responds materially to nitrogen and phosphorus supply; withholding nutrients to manufacture a fade is not evidence of normal development. | Color is not a validated harvest-maturity marker and this record does not recommend harvest timing, flushing, or a universal feeding concentration. | The source experiments used limited cultivars and defined production systems; their weeks and nutrient concentrations must not be generalized as thresholds. | No authoritative Cannabis photograph or video with adequate longitudinal measurements and causal exclusion was admitted; media remain empty rather than treating vendor, forum, anecdotal, or generated imagery as ground truth. | All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Cannabis reproductive sex expression
summary: Expressed sex is classified from reproductive organs, not seedling shape: pistillate flowers bear protruding stigmas, staminate flowers form stalked anther-bearing clusters, and co-sexual plants express both flower types or anthers within a pistillate inflorescence.
affectedParts: leaf axils and nodes | terminal and lateral inflorescences | flower bracts | stigmas | anthers
stages: seedling | vegetative | pre-flower | flower maturation
indicators: No reliable image-only sex distinction during the seedling or vegetative stage | Pistillate flowers with bifurcate protruding white-to-yellowish stigmas | Pedicillate clusters of staminate flowers that open to expose five anthers | Bright-yellow anthers within bract tissue among stigmas on a co-sexual inflorescence | Stigmas curl and brown or redden while bracts and carpels swell with pistillate-flower maturation
exclusions: A seedling or vegetative plant is labeled male or female from height, leaf size, vigor, or internode length alone | Only stipules, new axillary shoots, or unopened undifferentiated buds are visible | A single node or canopy view is used to exclude co-sexual expression | Yellow anther-like material is present but focus, scale, and surrounding flower organs are not visible | A Y-linked marker result is used to claim that female versus monoecious floral expression has been distinguished
lookAlikes: Stipules at the node | New axillary shoots | Unopened flower or leaf primordia | Swollen pistillate bracts | Senescing or damaged stigmas | Yellow plant debris or insect material inside an inflorescence
confirmation: Record focused macro views of several upper and lower nodes plus terminal and lateral inflorescences, including scale and the surrounding bract, stigma, or pedicel context. | Confirm pistillate expression from protruding stigmas and staminate expression from opened anther-bearing flowers rather than overall plant habit. | Repeat inspection through flowering because a few anthers can be hidden within dense pistillate tissue and may appear after an earlier negative view. | When pre-flower genetic sex is operationally important, use a validated Y-linked assay; interpret a negative result as female-or-monoecious genotype rather than proof of exclusively pistillate future expression.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label indeterminate when reproductive organs are not yet visible. | If pollen release matters to the production objective, isolate a plant with confirmed anthers while identity and facility-specific disposition are reviewed.
correctivePlan: Treat sex expression as a monitored developmental classification, not a nutrient or pesticide diagnosis. | Use serial, multi-location inspection to document whether staminate organs are isolated, plant-wide, or embedded within pistillate inflorescences. | Apply only the facility’s lawful crop-management protocol after expressed flower type is confirmed.
prevention: Include multiple-node macro imagery and time-series flowering views in capture protocols. | Maintain cultivar, propagation, photoperiod, treatment, and genetic-test records so expressed phenotype is not confused with genetic assay status. | Continue inspection of nominally female or marker-screened populations through flowering because co-sexual expression is not excluded by a single early observation.
warnings: Seedling silhouette, height, leaf number, leaf size, vigor, and internode length are not reliable ground-truth sex labels across cultivars. | A photograph of reproductive organs describes expressed floral phenotype at that place and time; it does not by itself establish chromosomal sex or guarantee future expression elsewhere on the plant. | The molecular assay cited here separates Y-bearing males from female or monoecious plants but cannot distinguish the latter two outcomes. | The CC BY figures are approved as reference displays and their licenses permit reuse, but they remain excluded from automated training until a separate dataset-split and leakage review.

name: Boron deficiency
summary: A controlled Cannabis boron-withholding disorder centered on growing tips, expanding leaves, and root tips. Severe new-growth distortion is useful supporting evidence, but diagnosis should be tied to nutrition and root-zone measurements rather than leaf shape alone.
affectedParts: growing tips | new and expanding leaves | leaf margins | root tips | whole plant in advanced cases
stages: vegetative | all
indicators: Growing tips become stunted before older foliage shows a dominant pattern | New leaflets are distorted, smaller, and narrow near the leaflet base | Advanced new growth curls inward, downward, or at irregular angles and develops marginal necrosis | Severe deficiency can kill growing tips and root tips and lead to whole-plant wilting
exclusions: Distorted tips contain broad mites or hemp russet mites | Root-zone boron supply and tissue analysis are adequate while another exposure explains the distortion | Damage is localized to a spray, heat, or mechanical event | Only old leaves are affected while new growth remains normal
lookAlikes: Calcium deficiency | Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Herbicide or growth-regulator injury | Root disease
confirmation: Review fertilizer and source-water boron and measure root-zone pH/EC before assigning the cause. | Use representative tissue analysis when the diagnosis is consequential; the published Cannabis values are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction root-zone and tissue measurements. | Inspect distorted growth under magnification for mites before changing nutrition.
correctivePlan: Correct a confirmed boron under-supply gradually with a crop-appropriate nutrition plan. | Track new meristem and root growth; damaged leaves and dead tips will not reverse.
prevention: Maintain complete micronutrient supply and calibrated root-zone monitoring. | Avoid diagnosing micronutrients from internet deficiency charts without measurements.
warnings: The controlled study used one cultivar and complete boron withholding. | Boron has a narrow adequacy-to-toxicity margin in many crops; do not add boron from visual suspicion alone.

name: Calcium deficiency
summary: A calcium-supply or transport disorder that can damage meristems, newly expanding leaves, roots, fan leaves, and sugar leaves. Controlled Cannabis studies produced different canopy-onset patterns, so spotting, curled tips, or marginal necrosis require feed, water, root-zone, tissue, stage, and cultivar evidence.
affectedParts: growing tips and newly expanding leaves in vegetative T1 | lower fan leaves at flowering-stage onset in Gelato 29 | upper fan leaves and sugar leaves as the Gelato 29 sequence advanced | leaflet bases, interveinal tissue, serrations, margins, and tips | root tips and root system | developing inflorescences and bracts for differential inspection
stages: vegetative growth | flowering | chronic insufficient supply or impaired transport
indicators: Vegetative T1: growing tips and new leaves become stunted and irregular while leaflet bases stay narrow and paler than tips | Vegetative T1 progression: basal yellowing intensifies into interveinal chlorosis, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, growing-tip death, and increased axillary branching | Flowering Gelato 29: lower fan leaves begin with interveinal yellow rings around necrotic brown centers during week three of withholding | Flowering Gelato 29 progression: spotting concentrates near margins and tips, coalesces into irregular marginal necrosis, and browns serration points | Later flowering progression: injury moves upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, with upward curling of upper fan-leaf tips | A calcium deficit or impaired calcium delivery is supported by input, root-zone, water, tissue, and plant-stage measurements linked to the imaged plant
exclusions: Spots, edge burn, or curl occur without a documented calcium-supply or transport problem | Root-zone EC is high and broad multi-ion salt injury explains the tip and margin damage | Roots are saturated, oxygen-limited, drought-stressed, temperature-injured, mechanically damaged, or diseased and calcium analysis does not support a deficit | Young-growth distortion is accompanied by mites, thrips, insects, webbing, eggs, fecal spots, or feeding scars | Discrete expanding lesions, halos, fungal structures, or laboratory results support a pathogen | Injury is limited to the hottest, brightest, sprayed, or contact-exposed canopy surfaces | Older-leaf marginal injury follows a potassium- or magnesium-type pattern and tissue/root-zone evidence supports that alternative | Yellowing is consistent with measured nitrogen deficiency or late-cycle senescence and no calcium evidence is present | Color or spotting is visible only under altered lighting, white balance, residue, dust, or compression artifact
lookAlikes: Potassium deficiency | Magnesium deficiency | Boron deficiency or toxicity | High-EC nutrient burn or salinity | Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia | Drought or excessive vapor demand | Cold or overheated root zone | Pythium or other root disease | Broad mite injury | Hemp russet mite injury | Thrips feeding injury | Heat or high-light injury | Foliar spray phytotoxicity | Leaf-spot pathogen | Normal late-flower senescence
confirmation: Do not confirm calcium deficiency from rust-colored spots, curled leaf tips, distorted new growth, marginal necrosis, one photograph, or one video. | Capture serial whole-plant, growing-tip, upper/middle/lower-canopy, fan-leaf, sugar-leaf, leaf upper-surface, underside, cleaned-root, and root-tip views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar plant. | Record the first affected node and leaf age, cultivar, stage, days since symptom onset, irrigation and dryback, root-zone water content, temperature, pH, EC, and dissolved oxygen where relevant. | Measure calcium and competing ions in source water, fertilizer stocks, final solution, root-zone extract, substrate or soil, and representative leaf tissue from defined upper and lower canopy positions. | Interpret tissue results using plant part, node, stage, cultivar, method, and system context; neither 0.39% from T1 nor the Gelato 29 upper/lower relationship is a universal threshold. | Inspect roots for active white tips, discoloration, softness, odor, lesions, binding, and mechanical damage; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when root pathogens or leaf lesions remain plausible. | Inspect distorted growth and both leaf surfaces with magnification for broad mites, russet mites, thrips, eggs, webbing, and feeding evidence. | Retain a suspected label until a calcium-supply or transport problem, compatible progression, and exclusion evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-treatment images, nutrient labels, mixing records, solution and water samples, root-zone readings, and representative tissue before changing the program. | Verify meter calibration, formulation calculations, source-water mineral content, root health, pH, EC, water status, and temperature before adding calcium or flushing. | Remove symptom-only samples from training-ground-truth collections until analytical and exposure evidence is reviewed.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified supply, pH, salinity, irrigation, temperature, oxygen, drainage, or root-health cause using crop-, medium-, and stage-appropriate agronomic guidance. | Restore a balanced nutrient solution rather than stacking unmeasured calcium-magnesium products; account for calcium already present in source water and fertilizers. | Track new growth, new roots, lesion rate, root-zone pH and EC, and follow-up tissue results; reopen potassium, magnesium, boron, pest, pathogen, and environmental differentials if response is absent.
prevention: Test source water and complete fertilizer for calcium and competing ions and document all calcium-containing inputs. | Use calibrated root-zone pH, EC, moisture, temperature, and irrigation monitoring appropriate to the production system. | Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent upper/lower canopy tissue-sampling and serial imaging procedures.
warnings: Controlled Cannabis studies disagreed on first affected canopy location: vegetative T1 began at growing tips and new leaves, while flowering Gelato 29 began on lower fan leaves; location alone is not ground truth. | The T1 five-week timing, 0.39% most-recent-mature-leaf value, and growing-tip sequence are experiment-specific. | The Gelato 29 three-week onset, upper/lower tissue relationship, and biomass response came from three deep-water-culture plants per treatment and must not be generalized. | Calcium can be present in the root zone while water status, salinity, temperature, oxygen, damaged roots, or transport conditions limit delivery; adding calcium does not correct those causes. | The CC BY figure is a single-treatment progression, but remains excluded from automated training until panel annotations, source grouping, and a leakage-safe dataset split are assigned. | The NC State e-GRO page requires author permission for its separate images; those assets were not copied or admitted. | All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Copper deficiency
summary: A controlled vegetative Cannabis copper-withholding response characterized by late-onset stunting, basal narrowing and yellowing of newer leaflets, progressive new-leaf distortion, fine interveinal chlorosis, slight inward/downward margin curl, and reduced turgidity. The evidence comes from one cultivar and requires tissue and root-zone confirmation.
affectedParts: whole plant for relative stunting | growing tips and newer foliage | newly expanding leaflets | leaflet bases | interveinal tissue | leaf margins | most-recent-mature leaves for source-comparable tissue analysis | roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative | late-onset deficiency | initial basal narrowing and yellowing | advanced distortion and fine interveinal chlorosis
indicators: Slight whole-plant stunting relative to a matched healthy plant | Newer and expanding leaves show mild distortion concentrated near leaflet bases | Leaflet bases become narrower than the distal leaflet and slightly yellow | Basal narrowing and distortion become more pronounced as the sequence advances | Marginal interveinal chlorosis develops on new and expanding leaves | Advanced leaves show fine interveinal chlorosis across much of the blade | Leaf margins distort and curl slightly inward and downward | New and expanding leaves show mildly reduced turgidity | Low copper is documented in correctly positioned foliage and linked to supply or root-zone availability

immediateActions: Stop discretionary boron-containing additives while preserving product labels, batch records, solution samples, pre-treatment images, and representative tissue for testing. | Verify source-water, stock, final-solution, root-zone, and tissue results before flushing or changing the complete nutrient program. | Separate suspect plants from training-ground-truth collections until the exposure and laboratory evidence are linked.
correctivePlan: Remove or correct the verified boron source and restore a balanced crop- and stage-appropriate nutrient solution using current local agronomic guidance. | Correct documented salinity, drainage, irrigation, pH, temperature, or root-health problems without assuming that every burned margin was caused by boron. | Track new growth, new-lesion rate, water or solution boron, EC and pH, and follow-up tissue results; reopen differentials if the expected exposure-response relationship is absent.
prevention: Test source water periodically for boron and salinity, especially after treatment-system, well, or reverse-osmosis changes. | Use verified mixing calculations and calibrated dosing equipment for micronutrient concentrates; record lot, concentration, date, and plant group. | Keep same-cultivar healthy references and consistent leaf-node tissue-sampling procedures so changes in leaf age or genotype are not mistaken for toxicity.
warnings: The T1 study induced toxicity with tenfold boron in one silica-sand system; its seven-week timing and 671.75 mg per kg tissue value are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds. | The White Shark report used three clones per treatment in deep-water culture; its three-week onset and canopy-wide distribution require replication across cultivars and production systems. | Marginal chlorosis and necrosis are highly nonspecific and must not become image-only ground truth. | The two source trials did not justify a universal yield-loss estimate; severe-looking leaf injury did not correspond to a clear yield loss in the small White Shark trial. | The CC BY figure contains both manganese- and boron-toxicity columns and is excluded from automated training until panel-level crops, labels, and dataset splits are reviewed. | The Niagara College project captured weekly 360-degree videos, but no original asset URLs or reuse license are publicly exposed; none are admitted as video references. | All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Manganese toxicity / high-manganese response
summary: A measurement-dependent Cannabis differential with conflicting published visual descriptions: a controlled T1 study reported lower-leaf marginal chlorosis progressing inward, while field diagnostic observations described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis. Neither pattern is specific enough for image- or video-only confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older leaves | leaflet margins | interveinal tissue | midrib-adjacent tissue as symptoms progress | whole canopy for distribution context
stages: vegetative | all
indicators: In the controlled T1 study, marginal yellowing began on lower leaves seven weeks after the high-Mn treatment | Controlled-study yellowing intensified inward toward the midrib; advanced leaves became severely chlorotic with necrotic margins and sometimes abscised | Separate field diagnostic observations described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis | A repeated canopy pattern plus measured fertilizer, water, root-zone, or tissue evidence supports abnormal manganese exposure; color alone does not
exclusions: Boron toxicity or potassium deficiency better explains the same older-leaf marginal chlorosis-to-necrosis sequence | High root-zone EC, water stress, root injury, or normal senescence explains the lower-canopy pattern | Discrete lesions, halos, fruiting bodies, or asymmetric spread support a leaf-spot pathogen instead of a nutrient exposure | Mite feeding, stippling, webbing, or visible arthropods explain fine chlorosis | No plausible manganese source, pH condition, or analytical abnormality is found
lookAlikes: Boron toxicity | Potassium deficiency | Salinity / high EC | Low-pH root-zone stress | Magnesium deficiency | Normal senescence | Leaf-spot disease | Spider-mite feeding
confirmation: Do not confirm manganese toxicity from an image or video. Capture standardized whole-canopy, upper/middle/lower-canopy, and both-surface close-ups over time; record leaf/node age and whether injury is marginal, interveinal, or lesion-centered. | Before correction, document fertilizer formulation and batch, injector settings, source-water chemistry, irrigation history, and root-zone pH and EC from representative affected and unaffected plants. | Use a defined-age representative tissue sample and interpret manganese with the analytical laboratory, cultivar, substrate, and crop stage; do not use 47.88 mg/kg as a universal toxicity threshold. | If lesions are discrete or spreading independently of exposure zones, submit fresh tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory and inspect both leaf surfaces under magnification for pathogens and mites.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction root-zone, input-water, fertilizer, and tissue evidence before changing the program. | Map affected plants against irrigation zones, stock tanks, substrate lots, and cultivar blocks, and isolate any suspected mixing or injector error.
