correctivePlan: Correct only a confirmed manganese source, formulation, injector, or root-zone pH problem using crop-appropriate professional guidance. | Track new leaves and repeated pH, EC, and tissue measurements; necrotic tissue and abscised leaves will not reverse.
prevention: Verify micronutrient formulation, stock-tank math, injector calibration, and source-water contribution. | Trend root-zone pH/EC and periodic tissue results by cultivar and stage instead of relying on a single visual threshold.
warnings: The controlled evidence used one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar, silica sand, and 180 micromolar Mn (tenfold the complete formula); its seven-week timing is not a universal field threshold. | Treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the study-cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range, and dry weight did not differ significantly from controls; the authors called for higher-concentration work. | The published visual patterns differ: the controlled study reported marginal injury and the field survey reported interveinal injury, so either pathway requires human review and analytical confirmation. | The licensed Figure 5 reference already stored under boron toxicity is a mixed-class composite with manganese in the left column and boron in the right; it is cross-reference context, not a clean manganese training sample, and is not duplicated here. | Visual chlorosis and necrosis are not manganese-specific, and no image or video in this record is ground truth.

name: Nitrogen toxicity
summary: A measurement-dependent Cannabis nitrogen disorder with two distinct controlled contexts: excessive total nitrogen during vegetative growth produced smaller dark-green shoots and restricted roots, while excessive ammonium fraction during reproductive growth caused growing-tip curl and marginal necrosis, later wilting, systemic necrosis, root damage, and possible plant death. These pathways must not be collapsed into a generic dark-leaf or claw label.
affectedParts: whole plant and organs for relative size | youngest fully developed fan leaves | growing tips and apical foliage under severe ammonium-form injury | leaf margins | stems and side branches | roots | apical and side inflorescences during reproductive-stage ammonium exposure | irrigation solution, leachate, substrate, and root zone for causal measurement
stages: vegetative total-nitrogen dose response | reproductive-stage nitrogen-form response | pre-symptomatic high-ammonium exposure | early severe ammonium injury | late cumulative ammonium injury
indicators: Documented nitrogen supply exceeds the crop, stage, cultivar, and production-system demand or the ammonium fraction is excessive relative to nitrate | At 320 mg/L total nitrogen in the controlled vegetative study, the whole plant, leaves, and roots were smaller than at the experiment optimum and foliage was dark green | Root restriction appeared at 240 mg/L total nitrogen even though shoot development and coloration remained visually similar to the 160 mg/L treatment | Dark-green color spans adequate and excessive total-nitrogen treatments and is supporting context only, never a diagnostic feature by itself | Under 100% ammonium at fixed total nitrogen, early apical growth was stunted and growing-tip leaves curled with marginal necrosis | Severe ammonium-form injury progressed from growing tips to widespread necrosis, wilting, severe root damage, and plant death | A 50% ammonium treatment remained visually normal through most of the experiment before necrosis and wilting appeared in the final two weeks | Serial measurements show reduced growth or biomass together with excess nitrogen exposure, elevated tissue nitrogen, high leachate nitrogen, or an excessive ammonium-to-nitrate ratio
exclusions: Dark green foliage is the only finding; the controlled total-nitrogen study showed similar color from 160 through 320 mg/L | Downward leaf clawing occurs without verified high nitrogen or ammonium exposure and without the published growth, root, or marginal-necrosis context | Root-zone EC or osmotic stress is high but nitrogen concentration, form, tissue status, and leachate do not isolate nitrogen from broad salinity injury | Growing tips are curled or necrotic and broad mites, russet mites, thrips, boron disorder, spray injury, heat, or light exposure explains the distribution better | Wilt follows drought, excessive vapor demand, waterlogging, root hypoxia, root temperature, or vascular/root disease without a nitrogen exposure-response link | Marginal necrosis follows a potassium, boron, salinity, contact, foliar-product, wind, or pathogen pattern and analytical evidence does not support nitrogen-form injury | Plants are small because of nitrogen deficiency, unsuitable pH, root binding, irrigation failure, cultivar architecture, stage, or another measured nutrient disorder | Color, gloss, or apparent curl changes only under grow lights, altered white balance, glare, shadow, lens distortion, compression, or stable genetic leaf form
lookAlikes: High-EC nutrient burn or broad salinity stress | Overwatering or root-zone hypoxia | Drought or excessive vapor demand | Heat or high-light injury | Cold or overheated root zone | Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease | Potassium deficiency | Boron deficiency or toxicity | Calcium deficiency | Broad mite injury | Hemp russet mite injury | Thrips injury | Foliar spray or plant-growth-regulator injury | Leaf-spot or vascular pathogen | Virus or viroid syndrome | Genetic leaf curl or compact architecture | Camera white-balance, exposure, glare, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm nitrogen toxicity from dark foliage, gloss, leaf clawing, tip burn, curl, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until nitrogen dose or form, root-zone measurements, and plant response are linked. | Separate suspected excessive total-nitrogen dose from suspected ammonium-form toxicity; record nitrate and ammonium concentrations and proportions rather than only a product EC or total fertilizer rate. | Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, growing tips, youngest fully developed leaves, both leaf surfaces and margins, stems, side branches, inflorescences when present, and washed roots under neutral repeatable lighting with scale and a healthy same-cultivar reference. | Record cultivar, stage, days since onset, complete fertilizer formulation, each nitrogen source, stock and injector calculations, water alkalinity, irrigation volume, drainage fraction, substrate or solution type, temperature, humidity, light, and recent product changes. | Measure calibrated input and representative root-zone or solution pH and EC, and test input, reservoir, leachate, or drainage for total nitrogen, nitrate, and ammonium as appropriate to the system; compare supply with actual water use and drainage. | Submit defined-position leaf tissue and appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret nitrogen with cultivar, stage, organ, method, salinity, and competing nutrients rather than using 160, 240, or 320 mg/L as universal thresholds. | Inspect growing tips and both leaf surfaces with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when mites, thrips, root disease, viruses, viroids, vascular pathogens, or foliar injury remain plausible. | Treat response of subsequent growth after a measured correction as supporting evidence only; it does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth nitrogen toxicity.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-treatment images, fertilizer labels, mixing records, solution samples, root-zone measurements, representative tissue, and matched healthy controls before changing the program. | Pause discretionary nitrogen-heavy additives while verifying total nitrogen, nitrate-to-ammonium ratio, pH, EC, irrigation, drainage, and root health; do not automatically flush an oxygen-limited or already saturated root zone. | Quarantine severe wilt or root decline from ground-truth collections and exclude infectious and arthropod causes before attributing the response to nutrition.
correctivePlan: When measurements confirm excessive total nitrogen, reduce cumulative nitrogen exposure gradually within a balanced crop-, cultivar-, stage-, and system-appropriate program under current local agronomic guidance. | When an excessive ammonium fraction is confirmed, correct nitrogen form as well as total concentration while monitoring pH movement, salinity, calcium, magnesium, potassium, roots, irrigation, and drainage. | Track subsequent root growth, apical leaf geometry, new marginal necrosis, plant expansion, root-zone and leachate chemistry, and follow-up tissue results; reopen differentials if the exposure-response relationship is absent.
prevention: Record nitrogen concentration and nitrate-to-ammonium ratio for source water, each fertilizer component, final solution, and representative tissue instead of relying on product dose or EC alone. | Calibrate dosing equipment and pH/EC meters, verify stock calculations, and monitor irrigation volume, drainage fraction, leachate chemistry, dryback, root-zone temperature, and oxygenation. | Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent node-, organ-, and stage-specific imaging and tissue sampling so naturally dark foliage or compact architecture is not mislabeled.
warnings: The vegetative dose study used one medical Cannabis cultivar, five plants per treatment, soilless media, long photoperiod, and a specific nutrient formulation; its 160 mg/L optimum and 240–320 mg/L restrictions are not universal Cannabis thresholds. | Irrigation EC increased with nitrogen dose in the vegetative study, so the highest-dose phenotype cannot be separated from treatment-specific salinity and ion-balance effects by an image. | The reproductive study held total nitrogen at 200 mg/L while exchanging nitrate for ammonium; high-ammonium injury is not interchangeable with excessive total nitrogen, and the authors noted that reduced or absent nitrate may contribute. | The 50% ammonium plants appeared normal for most of the experiment before late necrosis and wilting; a normal image cannot exclude a harmful nitrogen-form treatment or predict yield. | The controlled sources do not support dark clawed leaves, gloss, soft stems, burned tips, or delayed flowering as standalone Cannabis nitrogen-toxicity ground truth; those legacy claims were removed. | The dose-response Figure 1 combines five treatment columns and three organ/view rows and remains training-ineligible until every panel is dose-, organ-, time-, and source-group annotated with a leakage-safe split. | The 100% ammonium apical image is CC BY 4.0 but represents an extreme treatment confounded by nitrate absence; it remains training-ineligible and requires human scientific review. | All symptom-only, dark-leaf-only, claw-only, and unmeasured-EC samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Downy mildew
summary: A foliar oomycete disease of Cannabis. Angular chlorotic-to-brown lesions and dark underside sporulation are stronger clues than top-surface discoloration alone.
affectedParts: older inner-canopy leaves first in documented field observations | upper leaf surface | lower leaf surface directly beneath lesions | younger and upper-canopy leaves as disease progresses | whole canopy through defoliation | inflorescences in the New York field report
stages: vegetative | flower | closed-canopy field production | humid or extended-leaf-wetness periods | early-morning sporulation window
indicators: Early upper-surface lesions are yellow-green or reddish-brown, irregular, and may carry an uneven light-green or yellow halo. | Expanding lesions become brown, angular or elongated, and visibly bounded by leaf veins rather than remaining uniformly circular. | Corresponding lower-surface lesions can bear purplish-gray to gray-black down-like sporulation during wet, humid periods. | Underside sporulation can be transient: Ontario field guidance reports it most often in the morning before wind dispersal, so a midday absence is weak negative evidence. | Documented field distribution began on older leaves in the humid inner canopy and moved upward as disease progressed. | Heavily lesioned leaves can distort, curl, necrose, and fall, producing progressive lower- or inner-canopy thinning. | Multiple cultivars were affected in the New York field report, but a 108-entry assay showed susceptibility from 0 to 100%, so severity and visibility are genotype-dependent. | Leaves and inflorescences were affected in the New York report; Ontario observations found no flower or seed-head injury in that outbreak, so floral involvement is possible but not required.
exclusions: White superficial colonies on either leaf surface, especially if they wipe or scrape away, fit powdery mildew better than downy mildew. | Black pepper-like pycnidia embedded in lesions support Septoria rather than Pseudoperonospora. | Orange underside pustules or spores support rust rather than gray-black downy-mildew sporulation. | Lower-surface sooty material identified as Pseudocercospora conidiophores and conidia excludes a Pseudoperonospora species label for that sampled lesion. | A uniform exposure-edge, spray-track, droplet, or contact pattern with no organism evidence supports chemical or physical injury. | General interveinal chlorosis without discrete vein-bounded lesions or corresponding underside signs supports a nutrient or root-zone differential. | Mites, thrips, frass, residue, or necrotic tissue explain the dark underside material under magnification. | A negative midday underside photograph does not exclude downy mildew; repeat the inspection while leaves are wet and before early-morning sporulation disperses.
lookAlikes: Septoria leaf spot | Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot | Cercospora leaf spot | Alternaria leaf spot | Bipolaris leaf spot or blight | Rust | Powdery mildew | Bacterial leaf spot | Two-spotted spider mite or thrips injury | Spray, contact, or droplet injury | Nutrient or root-zone chlorosis | Normal late-season senescence
confirmation: Capture the same attached lesion from the upper surface and directly corresponding lower surface, plus whole-plant and canopy-location context; include a scale, leaf age, crop stage, and whether veins bound the lesion. | Inspect before the first winds of the day while leaves are still wet or humid, then repeat after drying to document whether underside fuzz was transient; do not treat a midday negative as definitive. | Use a hand lens or microscope to separate branching sporangiophores and sporangia from pycnidia, conidia, rust pustules, insects, frass, residue, and necrotic tissue. | Submit multiple actively developing, plant-linked lesions with matched upper/lower images and collection metadata to a plant diagnostic laboratory; preserve several asymptomatic comparison leaves from the same area. | Confirm Pseudoperonospora cannabina with oomycete morphology plus validated molecular evidence; the New York report used ITS, cox2, and ypt1 and confirmed a reisolate after pathogenicity testing. | Retain cultivar, assay type, tissue type, inoculation or field context, time of day, humidity or leaf wetness, and sampling location with every image label because these factors change symptom visibility and severity estimates. | Keep symptom-only, upper-surface-only, midday-underside-only, detached-stock-photo, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed downy-mildew class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph distribution and matched leaf surfaces before disturbing the canopy, preferably during the early-morning sporulation window. | Separate heavily symptomatic material where operationally appropriate, preserve fresh diagnostic samples, and avoid moving wet symptomatic foliage through unaffected areas. | Record recent dew, rainfall, irrigation, leaf-wetness duration, canopy closure, airflow, cultivar, and whether symptoms cluster in older humid inner-canopy leaves.
correctivePlan: Base disease-management decisions on a confirmed oomycete diagnosis and products or practices legally permitted for the crop, jurisdiction, and production setting. | Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and improve foliage drying or airflow where feasible, while recognizing that an environmental response does not retroactively confirm the pathogen. | Mark lesions and repeat upper/lower/canopy captures to distinguish new infection, transient sporulation, lesion aging, and leaf loss.
prevention: Scout older inner-canopy leaves and their undersides as canopies close, with extra attention after extended dew, rain, misting, or other leaf-wetness periods. | Maintain sanitation and airflow practices that limit prolonged canopy humidity and avoid unnecessary wetting of foliage. | Keep cultivar identity and source-lot metadata because the controlled germplasm study documented extreme susceptibility differences.
warnings: Pseudoperonospora is an oomycete, not a true fungus; a generic mildew label can lead to incorrect organism and management assumptions. | Vein-limited brown lesions, yellow halos, and underside dark growth overlap other pathogens and injuries and do not establish species without plant-linked organism evidence. | Underside sporulation may be absent by midday, after drying, or in a single frame; time of day and wetness must accompany negative observations. | The 2026 resistance study used leaf-disc, detached-leaf, visual, and CNN phenotyping methods that produced different severity estimates; those scores are not universal production-image thresholds. | Field reports disagree on whether reproductive tissue is visibly affected, so flower or seed-head involvement is neither required nor safe to infer from foliar severity. | The two Ontario photographs are credited but lack explicit reusable or automated-training rights. They remain metadata-only, hidden from display, and training-prohibited; no media file is copied. | No photo or video is ground truth without linked sampling and organism confirmation; all symptom-only, rights-unclear, mixed-organism, and low-resolution samples require human review.

name: Cannabis aphid
summary: A Cannabis-adapted aphid found on hemp leaves and stems indoors and outdoors. Confirm by observing and identifying the insect; generalized curling, yellowing, or reduced vigor is not species-level evidence.
affectedParts: leaf undersides | petioles | stems | shoot tips | whole canopy when populations are heavy
stages: vegetative | flower | all
indicators: Colonies of small soft-bodied aphids are visible on cannabis leaves or stems | Wingless aphids show pale abdominal striping while winged forms may show dark spotting | Aphid cast skins or sticky honeydew occur near an active colony | New growth is stressed in the same areas where aphids are actively feeding
exclusions: No aphids, cast skins, or honeydew are found after repeated underside and stem inspection | Only roots contain aphids while foliage and stems are free of colonies | Fine stippling, webbing, mites, or eggs dominate the underside evidence | Silvery feeding scars with dark fecal specks support thrips instead
lookAlikes: Rice root aphid | Thrips | Two-spotted spider mites | Whitefly or another phloem-feeding insect
confirmation: Inspect leaf undersides, petioles, stems, and shoot tips with magnification and document intact aphids. | Use morphological identification or an entomology reference when species-level identification matters; body color alone is not diagnostic.
immediateActions: Separate heavily infested material from clean propagation stock and inspect neighboring plants. | Record where colonies occur and preserve clear close-up images or a specimen before treatment.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated pest-management response appropriate to the production system and local pesticide/biocontrol rules. | Reinspect new growth and undersides after intervention rather than judging success from old damaged tissue.
prevention: Inspect incoming clones and mother-stock material before integration. | Use routine underside and stem scouting so small colonies are detected before they spread.
warnings: Do not identify Phorodon cannabis from leaf yellowing, curling, or aphid color alone. | Do not assume every aphid found around the root zone is cannabis aphid; rice root aphid is a distinct Cannabis-associated pest.

name: Fungus gnats / root-feeding Bradysia larvae
summary: A greenhouse root-zone pest complex in which adult fungus gnats signal moist-media populations and larvae can feed on roots and interact with soil-borne disease. Evidence is cross-crop greenhouse literature, so Cannabis symptoms alone are not diagnostic.
affectedParts: growing medium surface | roots | lower stem | whole plant secondarily
stages: seedling | vegetative | flower | all
indicators: Small dark gnat-like adults repeatedly emerge from or rest near moist growing media | Translucent slender larvae with dark head capsules are found in the root zone | Poor growth or yellowing occurs together with confirmed fungus-gnat larvae in wet organic media
exclusions: No adults or larvae are found after sticky-card and root-zone inspection | Root-associated aphids rather than fly larvae are present | Root decay is confirmed without fungus-gnat larvae | Canopy symptoms track a measured nutrient, pH, EC, light, or irrigation problem instead
lookAlikes: Rice root aphid | Pythium root rot | Fusarium crown and root rot | Overwatering / low root-zone oxygen
confirmation: Use sticky cards for adults and inspect moist media/root zones for characteristic larvae. | Confirm root health independently because fungus gnats may coexist with soil-borne pathogens.
immediateActions: Inspect moisture management, algae, plant debris, and the root zone. | Document adults and larvae before attributing canopy symptoms to fungus gnats.
correctivePlan: Use sanitation, moisture management, physical or biological controls that are appropriate to the crop system and local rules. | Continue monitoring adults and larvae while separately tracking root recovery.
prevention: Avoid chronic surface wetness and remove algae and decomposing plant debris. | Monitor greenhouse/media pest pressure before symptoms appear.
warnings: This profile uses greenhouse cross-crop evidence for Bradysia biology; it does not make generic yellowing a Cannabis-specific fungus-gnat signature. | Do not treat a few adult gnats as proof that they are the primary cause of a major root or canopy disorder.

name: Rice root aphid on cannabis
summary: A root-associated aphid that has become a common host-associated pest of indoor Cannabis in North America. Root-zone insect evidence is required because above-ground decline is nonspecific.
affectedParts: roots | growing medium surface | root-zone container | whole plant secondarily
stages: vegetative | flower | late flower | all
indicators: Aphid colonies are visible on cannabis roots after careful root-zone inspection | Winged aphids emerge from or cluster around the growing medium while root colonies are present | Root-associated aphids are documented while stems and leaf undersides lack the typical cannabis-aphid colony pattern
exclusions: No aphids are found on roots after representative inspection of the root ball or root zone | Aphids are concentrated on leaves and stems rather than roots | Small dark flies and translucent black-headed larvae support fungus gnats instead | Brown slimy roots and wilt occur without root aphids and a root pathogen or oxygen problem explains the decline better
lookAlikes: Cannabis aphid | Fungus gnats | Root pathogen | Water / root-zone stress
confirmation: Expose representative roots and document aphids directly associated with roots. | Use morphological identification when distinguishing rice root aphid from other aphids is operationally important.
immediateActions: Inspect nearby root zones and isolate infested propagation material where practical. | Record root condition separately so root feeding is not confused with concurrent root disease or irrigation stress.
correctivePlan: Use a root-zone IPM plan appropriate to the production system and local rules. | Verify population decline by repeat root inspection rather than relying only on fewer flying adults.
prevention: Inspect root balls of incoming plants and rooted cuttings. | Include root-zone scouting when unexplained flying aphids appear indoors.
warnings: Do not diagnose rice root aphid from yellowing, stunting, or flying insects alone. | Root aphids and root disease can coexist; finding one does not exclude the other.

name: Hemp witches’ broom (phytoplasma-associated)
scientificName: Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii and other phytoplasmas
summary: A leafhopper-associated systemic syndrome in which cannabis can develop shortened nodes, clusters of proliferating axillary or apical shoots, stunting, small distorted leaves, chlorosis, mottling, and curling; the same visual pattern can involve Beet curly top virus, Spiroplasma citri, or mixed infection.
affectedParts: young and expanding leaves | upper and lower leaf surfaces | leaf petioles | axillary buds | apical shoots | stems and internodes | whole-plant architecture
stages: field-grown leaf-bearing plants; cannabis-specific stage effects are not established
indicators: Clusters of excessive apical or axillary shoots forming a broom-like tip | Shortened internodes and compact branch clusters | Small, distorted, curled, or upward-rolled leaves | Leaf chlorosis with mottling or mosaic | Vein-bounded green islands on the upper leaf surface | Interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance from below | Whole-plant stunting with abnormal branching
exclusions: Validated testing identifies Beet curly top virus without detecting phytoplasma in properly sampled tissue | Validated testing identifies Spiroplasma citri or another agent and does not detect phytoplasma | Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in the distorted growing tips | Abnormal branching follows deliberate topping or training and subsequent leaves remain normal | Distortion maps to documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure | Short internodes and branching remain stable in healthy clones without chlorosis, mottling, progressive distortion, or pathogen detection
lookAlikes: Beet curly top virus disease | Spiroplasma citri infection | Mixed BCTV-phytoplasma-Spiroplasma infection | Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury | Topping or high-stress training response | Genetic dwarfism or fasciation | Micronutrient or root-zone disorder | Mosaic virus complex
confirmation: Do not confirm phytoplasma from witches’ broom architecture, a photograph, video, or leafhopper observation. | Submit the most symptomatic young leaves with petioles to a plant diagnostic laboratory using that laboratory’s current sampling and shipping protocol; include a healthy comparator when requested. | Use a validated phytoplasma molecular assay followed by sequence or classification evidence when group-level identity matters; the Nevada report combined real-time PCR, nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis. | Request a differential panel that includes Beet curly top virus and Spiroplasma citri because the three agents can produce overlapping symptoms and can occur together. | Record whole-plant architecture, both leaf surfaces, affected shoot position, field location, onset date, and serial change to preserve image and video context without treating those observations as proof.
immediateActions: Flag suspect plants and pause distribution of their cuttings pending laboratory results. | Scout nearby plants and leafhoppers while keeping vector presence separate from pathogen confirmation. | Keep all symptom-only images out of phytoplasma, Spiroplasma, and BCTV ground-truth classes.
correctivePlan: Base removal and vector-management decisions on laboratory results, production policy, and locally legal recommendations. | If phytoplasma is not detected, continue testing or differential review for BCTV, Spiroplasma citri, mites, chemical injury, and physiological causes. | Continue serial observation because one plant or branch can combine architecture, foliar color, and distortion differently over time.
prevention: Use tested and traceable propagation material. | Monitor leafhoppers and regional alerts without assuming every vector carries the same pathogen. | Control weed reservoirs and vectors only with locally appropriate, crop-legal practices.
warnings: Witches’ broom is a syndrome, not a species-level visual diagnosis. | Cannabis symptom overlap and documented mixed infections make image-only ground truth unsafe. | The three institutional photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden and prohibited from automated training. | Cannabis-specific evidence does not establish a universal symptom order, cultivar response, or infection-to-symptom interval.

name: Root binding / container-restriction stress
summary: Container restriction is documented in hemp transplants, but canopy stress is nonspecific and roots touching a pot are not sufficient evidence. A defensible label requires plant-linked views of the intact root ball, repeatable boundary-following deformation or dense matting, and exclusion of dry-center irrigation failure, salinity, hypoxia, transplant injury, nematodes, and root disease.
affectedParts: root-ball perimeter and bottom | root-ball center | root tips | crown and lower stem for exclusions | whole plant secondarily
stages: seedling | transplant | vegetative | post-transplant establishment
indicators: Multiple roots follow the container wall or bottom in repeated arcs, coils, or a dense boundary mat rather than extending radially through available substrate. | The extracted intact root mass retains the container geometry and shows a tight root-dominant perimeter across more than one face; one exposed root or a cohesive nursery root ball is insufficient. | The root-ball center and perimeter differ visibly in moisture after a documented irrigation event, consistent with preferential flow or incomplete wetting; this supports a water-delivery mechanism but is not specific to root binding. | A plant-linked whole-canopy comparison may show reduced expansion or vigor relative to a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-zone control, but canopy appearance is secondary evidence only. | In field-transplanted hemp, the original root architecture may remain constrained after transplant and poor establishment can coexist with secondary Fusarium or Pythium infection. | Time-matched root views show increasing wall-following deflection or matting before any post-transplant establishment failure, preserving the temporal link between container occupancy and later stress.
exclusions: Do not label a plant from canopy stunting, wilt, chlorosis, marginal browning, or reduced vigor without a plant-linked intact root-ball inspection. | Do not treat a small container, roots visible at drainage holes, one perimeter root, or normal root-ball cohesion as proof of pathological restriction. | Exclude drought or irrigation channeling with measured center-versus-edge moisture before and after irrigation and a documented wetting pattern. | Exclude salinity or fertilizer concentration with calibrated root-zone EC and input/runoff records. | Exclude overwatering or hypoxia with moisture history, aeration context, odor, root color, and tissue integrity rather than inferring it from wilt alone. | Escalate brown, water-soaked, sloughed, necrotic, lesioned, or foul-smelling roots for culture or molecular testing for Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and other root pathogens. | Inspect washed roots for discrete galls or abnormal swellings and obtain nematode confirmation when root-knot nematodes remain plausible. | Exclude transplant shock, torn roots, compressed plugs, buried crowns, stem girdling, and container heat injury using handling history and crown/root inspection.
lookAlikes: Normal cohesive nursery root ball or vigorous roots at drainage holes | Drought / water-deficit stress | Irrigation channeling or hydrophobic substrate without mechanical root restriction | Salinity / high EC | Overwatering / root-zone hypoxia | Pythium root rot | Fusarium or Rhizoctonia crown/root disease | Root-knot nematodes | Transplant shock or mechanical root tearing | Container-side heat injury | Stem girdling, buried crown, or compressed propagation plug | Nutrient deficiency caused by pH or root-zone chemistry
confirmation: Before disturbing roots, record a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy, container size and shape, substrate surface, drainage openings, crown, and all accessible root-ball faces with a metric scale and neutral color reference. | Extract the root ball intact and photograph the top, bottom, and at least four side quadrants; then gently remove substrate and repeat the views so normal cohesion can be separated from repeated container-contour roots. | Capture a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-substrate, same-irrigation comparison plant using identical views and exposure; do not infer restriction from an unmatched small-pot image. | Measure root-zone moisture at the center and perimeter immediately before and after a documented irrigation event, and record input and leachate EC plus pH with calibrated instruments. | Document root color, firmness, odor, lesions, sloughing, crown integrity, and discrete galls; submit representative plant-linked tissue for pathogen or nematode testing when those signs are present. | For a post-transplant sequence, keep plant identity linked across dates and include the original root-ball boundary plus new roots beyond it; do not use canopy recovery or failure alone as confirmation. | Keep canopy-only, detached-root-only, non-Cannabis transfer, unmatched, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear samples out of the confirmed class and all automated training splits.
immediateActions: Preserve and document at least one intact symptomatic root ball and one matched comparison before cutting, teasing, washing, transplanting, or changing irrigation. | Measure center/perimeter moisture, EC, pH, and drainage behavior while screening for root decay and galls; avoid assigning the cause from pot size or canopy appearance. | Quarantine or segregate plants with root lesions, decay, or galls until infectious and nematode differentials are evaluated.
correctivePlan: Use crop-stage- and production-system-appropriate transplant or root-management practices only after physical restriction is confirmed; the non-Cannabis sources do not validate a universal Cannabis root-pruning method. | Correct verified irrigation nonuniformity, salinity, hypoxia, or infection as separate coexisting problems rather than assuming that relieving container restriction resolves them. | Track new roots beyond the former container boundary and compare canopy development with matched controls; retain the record as uncertain if root expansion and plant response are not temporally linked.
prevention: Match container volume and transplant timing to cultivar growth rate and production duration, and audit representative intact root balls before transplant batches are moved. | Record container history, up-pot dates, irrigation delivery, substrate, cultivar, and plant age so boundary deformation can be interpreted against an appropriate comparison. | Reject or flag incoming transplants with severe repeated circling/matting, decay, galls, or an undocumented root-zone history for human review.
warnings: Photo or video alone cannot establish the physiological cause of canopy stress; root-ball morphology, plant linkage, measurements, and exclusion checks are required. | The controlled rooting-volume meta-analysis and University of Maryland morphology guide are non-Cannabis transfer evidence and do not establish Cannabis thresholds, universal symptoms, severity, or treatment efficacy. | The hemp evidence is a diagnostic survey rather than a controlled container-size trial, so cultivar response, incidence, timing, yield effect, and a pathological root-density threshold remain unresolved. | Root binding can coexist with Fusarium, Pythium, irrigation failure, or salinity; finding circling roots does not exclude a more proximate cause of decline. | No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis root-binding progression image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch; media remains an explicit gap rather than using vendor, anecdotal, or non-Cannabis imagery as ground truth.

name: Fusarium crown and root rot / wilt complex
summary: A Cannabis crown/root/wilt disease complex associated with multiple Fusarium species. Yellowing and wilt are nonspecific; dark sunken crown tissue, root necrosis, and internal discoloration increase suspicion, while laboratory isolation or molecular work is required for organism-level confirmation.
affectedParts: roots | crown | lower stem | vascular and pith tissues | whole canopy secondarily
stages: propagation | vegetative | flower | all
indicators: Dark sunken crown lesions extend upward from the cannabis root zone | Reddish-brown or dark internal stem discoloration originates at the crown | Roots are necrotic while crown tissue is darkened or rotted | Canopy yellowing and wilt occur together with documented crown or internal stem decay
exclusions: Roots and crown are firm and healthy with no internal discoloration | Brown slimy roots occur without crown or internal stem lesions and Pythium or oxygen stress is better supported | Wilt resolves promptly after correcting a documented irrigation deficit without crown decay | Only one-sided mechanical stem injury explains the crown discoloration
lookAlikes: Pythium root rot | Severe drought or irrigation failure | Root-zone hypoxia / overwatering | Vascular or bacterial disease
confirmation: Inspect roots, crown, and a clean stem cross-section for the distribution of decay and internal discoloration. | Use a plant-diagnostic laboratory for isolation plus molecular or sequence-based identification when Fusarium confirmation changes management.
immediateActions: Quarantine severely affected plants and avoid moving contaminated root-zone material or runoff to clean plants. | Document crown/root/internal symptoms before destructive sampling and preserve representative tissue for diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation, culling, irrigation-system, and crop-protection decisions on confirmed pathogen and production-system evidence. | Inspect propagation stock and adjacent plants because Fusarium can move through infected plant material and contaminated production environments.
prevention: Start with clean propagation stock and sanitized tools, containers, and root-zone systems. | Prevent recirculation or movement of contaminated irrigation water where pathogen spread is a concern.
warnings: A photograph of yellowing or wilt cannot confirm Fusarium. | Multiple Fusarium species and Pythium can occur in similar Cannabis crown/root disease complexes; do not make species-level claims without laboratory evidence. | The Fusarium species list on Cannabis continues to expand; a model should rank a Fusarium syndrome separately from a laboratory-confirmed species label.

name: Acidic or extreme substrate-pH root stress
summary: A measured root-zone condition in which persistently acidic peat-based substrate suppresses Cannabis shoot and root development, while either acidic or high-pH extremes can restrict visible root growth. There is no unique leaf appearance: cultivar, fertility, EC, substrate, and exposure duration materially change what a camera can see.
affectedParts: root tips and developing root system | whole-plant diameter and shoot biomass | lower foliage when low pH is combined with excessive micronutrient fertility in a susceptible cultivar | leaf tips and leaflet interior during treatment-associated bronzing and necrosis | root-zone solution and substrate for direct pH and EC measurement
stages: root establishment | vegetative growth | chronic root-zone exposure
indicators: Repeated calibrated substrate measurements remain at an extreme rather than a single irrigation or runoff reading | Root-tip development is reduced relative to matched healthy plants before a specific foliar pattern is reliable | Whole-plant diameter and accumulated shoot biomass lag despite plant height sometimes remaining similar | At acidic pH, leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations may rise without visible toxicity | In the Sweetened pH 3.8 plus fourfold-micronutrient treatment, lower-leaf tips bronzed, became necrotic, spread inward, and developed chlorosis | The same low-pH and high-micronutrient treatment did not produce the same foliage response in Cherry Wine
exclusions: Only nutrient-solution input pH was measured and the actual substrate or root-zone pH is unknown | A single runoff, reservoir, or slurry reading is outside target but repeat representative measurements are not | High EC, fertilizer imbalance, or source-water alkalinity explains the response without a persistent measured substrate-pH extreme | Roots are restricted by saturation, compaction, container binding, drought, temperature, oxygen limitation, transplant damage, or root disease | Foliar bronzing or necrosis is localized to heat, light, spray, contact, pest feeding, or infectious lesions | Tissue analysis supports a specific nutrient deficiency or toxicity and measured root-zone pH is not outside the production-system target | Color differences appear only under altered lighting, white balance, cultivar pigmentation, senescence, or compression artifact
lookAlikes: Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia | High-EC nutrient burn or salinity | Water shortage or drought | Cold or overheated root zone | Root binding or compacted substrate | Pythium root rot | Phytophthora root rot | Fusarium crown or root disease | Micronutrient toxicity | Phosphorus deficiency | Potassium deficiency | Heat or high-light injury | Foliar spray phytotoxicity | Normal late-flower senescence
confirmation: Do not diagnose pH stress from leaf color, tip burn, stunting, one photograph, one video, or a generic nutrient-availability chart. | Measure the actual substrate or root-zone pH repeatedly with a calibrated meter and a method appropriate to the medium; record sampling location, depth, irrigation timing, extraction method, meter calibration, temperature, and replicate values. | Measure root-zone and input EC alongside pH, and document source-water pH and alkalinity, fertilizer formulation, acid or base additions, lime charge, substrate batch, irrigation volume, leaching fraction, and drainage. | Capture serial whole-plant top and side views, root-zone and cleaned-root views, upper- and lower-canopy views, and close-ups of both leaf surfaces under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar control. | Record cultivar, plant age, stage, days of exposure, container volume, substrate composition, water content, root-zone temperature, dissolved oxygen where relevant, and root-tip quantity or standardized root coverage. | Use representative leaf-tissue and root-zone or substrate analysis to separate a pH-associated exposure from a specific nutrient disorder; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when discolored or decaying roots, lesions, or pests remain plausible. | Retain a measured-exposure or suspected label unless the pH history, root or growth response, competing exposures, and analytical evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction pH, EC, alkalinity, solution, substrate, tissue, root, and image records before changing the system. | Verify the measuring method and calibration with repeat samples; avoid large unmeasured acid, base, lime, fertilizer, or flush corrections. | Quarantine uncertain images and videos from diagnostic ground truth until exposure and confounder evidence is linked.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified cause gradually using substrate- and water-appropriate guidance, considering alkalinity and buffering rather than input pH alone. | Restore a balanced fertilizer and irrigation program while monitoring substrate pH, EC, water content, drainage, and new root growth. | Reassess root pathogens, salinity, water status, temperature, and nutrient-specific differentials if new root tips and growth do not improve after the measured pH returns to the intended range.
prevention: Establish a production-system-specific substrate pH and EC monitoring protocol with calibrated meters, consistent extraction methods, replicate sampling, and trend alerts. | Test source-water alkalinity and account for substrate lime and fertilizer acidity before making recurring pH adjustments. | Keep same-cultivar controls and serial root and canopy images so gradual growth restriction is not mistaken for a specific leaf disorder.
warnings: The study supports a measured substrate-pH stress record, not a universal image phenotype or a universal nutrient-lockout chart. | The 5.5 to 6.5 recommendation came from peat-based greenhouse experiments and must not be copied unchanged to soil, field, coco, rockwool, aeroponic, or deep-water systems. | At normal micronutrient supply, low pH increased tissue accumulation without a universal visible toxicity; absence of bronzing does not establish that the root zone is acceptable. | The lower-leaf bronzing sequence occurred in Sweetened under pH 3.8 plus fourfold micronutrients and was absent in Cherry Wine; it is not low-pH-specific ground truth. | A single runoff or reservoir pH value does not prove the pH experienced throughout the root system. | No image or video is admitted for this record because no stable original asset URL was independently verified during this review. | All symptom-only or uncalibrated-pH samples remain low confidence and require human review.

name: Pythium root rot
summary: An oomycete root disease favored by wet, low-oxygen conditions; affected roots discolor, soften, and lose function.
affectedParts: roots | crown | whole plant
stages: all
indicators: Brown slimy roots | Wilting despite moisture | Stunting and yellowing | Crown rot in severe cases
exclusions: Roots are tan from media staining but firm | Container is very light and dry | Only one leaf shows damage
lookAlikes: Overwatering or root hypoxia | Phytophthora root rot | Fusarium crown disease
confirmation: Inspect cleaned roots for texture and active white tips. | Laboratory testing is required to distinguish similar root pathogens.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone water and tools. | Restore oxygenation and correct saturation.
correctivePlan: Remove irrecoverable plants where appropriate and sanitize wetted equipment. | Use only legal crop-appropriate treatments.
prevention: Control water temperature, sanitation, oxygen, and irrigation duration.
warnings: Visual symptoms cannot reliably identify Pythium to species. | Pythium species differ in temperature and production-system ecology; do not treat one environmental threshold as universal for the entire complex.

name: Rhizoctonia sore shin / root and crown rot
summary: A Cannabis root/crown disease documented as wilting with necrotic lesions at the plant base just above the soil line. Characteristic right-angle branching hyphae and laboratory identification are needed because the canopy response overlaps other root diseases.
affectedParts: roots | crown | lower stem just above soil line | whole plant
stages: seedling | transplant | vegetative | reproductive
indicators: Plants wilt while necrotic lesions develop at the stem base near the soil line | Roots/crown show compatible necrotic disease | Pigmented septate hyphae from lesions branch at roughly 90 degrees with basal constriction | ITS/18S or other laboratory evidence supports Rhizoctonia solani
exclusions: White cottony basal mycelium with round brown sclerotia strongly supports southern blight | Soft/slimy roots and oomycete evidence support Pythium | Vascular discoloration and Fusarium evidence support Fusarium wilt/crown disease | No basal/root lesions exist and water-status measurements explain wilt
lookAlikes: Southern blight | Pythium root rot | Fusarium crown/root rot | Root binding | Drought / water-deficit stress
confirmation: Inspect and photograph roots/crown and lower-stem lesions; submit lesion tissue for fungal morphology and molecular identification. | Do not confirm Rhizoctonia from wilted foliage alone.
immediateActions: Separate suspect root-zone material and preserve a fresh lesion sample. | Check irrigation/moisture and root binding concurrently.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed root-disease sanitation and crop-appropriate management. | Correct measured root-zone stressors that may worsen disease.
prevention: Use clean media/containers and avoid moving contaminated soil. | Inspect transplants for crown lesions and bound/diseased roots.
warnings: Rhizoctonia can coexist with other root stresses/pathogens. | Canopy wilt is not organism-specific.

name: White root rot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed hemp root disease characterized by declining canopy tissue together with white root-surface mycelium and fan-like mycelial growth beneath root bark. Root signs are essential because yellowing and wilt are nonspecific.
affectedParts: roots | root bark | root crown secondarily | whole canopy
stages: vegetative | flower | field production
indicators: Roots are covered by conspicuous white fungal mycelium | Fan-like mycelial growth occurs beneath root bark | Canopy yellowing and apical wilt progress rapidly in a plant with compatible root signs | Laboratory morphology and molecular evidence identify Dematophora/Rosellinia necatrix
exclusions: No white or fan-like root mycelium is present and another root pathogen is confirmed | White cottony growth and spherical basal sclerotia support southern blight | Small black crown sclerotia support Sclerotinia crown rot | Wilt occurs with physically healthy roots and a measured water deficit explains symptoms
lookAlikes: Southern blight | Sclerotinia crown rot | Pythium root rot | Fusarium crown/root rot | Rhizoctonia root rot
confirmation: Expose and photograph roots before cleaning, then inspect beneath bark for fan-like mycelium. | Use culture and molecular identification for organism-level confirmation.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone soil, tools, and debris from clean production areas. | Preserve representative colonized roots for laboratory diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation, culling, soil/root-zone management, and crop-protection decisions on confirmed disease and locally legal options.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil and infected root debris. | Inspect planting sites with a history of susceptible perennial crops or unexplained root-rot mortality.
warnings: Canopy wilt or chlorosis cannot diagnose white root rot. | White fungal growth must be interpreted at the root/crown location and distinguished from other soilborne fungi.

name: Drought / water-deficit stress
summary: Water deficit is a measured exposure-response diagnosis, not a synonym for drooping leaves. Cannabis studies document leaf-angle change, chlorosis, reduced expansion, cultivar-specific wilting or shedding, and growth or yield effects, but the label requires plant-linked root-zone moisture and irrigation history plus exclusion of salinity, hypoxia, heat/VPD, root restriction, vascular injury, and root disease.
affectedParts: root-zone center and perimeter | fan leaves and petioles | older foliage | newer foliage in sustained stress | shoot tips and whole canopy | flowers, biomass, and yield secondarily
stages: seedling | vegetative | flower | post-transplant establishment
indicators: Substrate or soil moisture is measurably below the established irrigation target while the plant shows water-deficit stress | Canopy wilt or reduced expansion coincides with a documented dry root zone and improves after appropriate rehydration | Leaf area or biomass growth declines during a sustained measured water deficit without root rot evidence | A time-linked root-zone measurement shows water content below that plant and production system's established irrigated baseline while leaf posture or growth changes develop. | Repeated side-view images show fan-leaf blades and petioles moving downward relative to their own turgid baseline and a matched irrigated control; absolute leaf angle from one frame is not diagnostic. | The temporal pattern begins after a documented missed, blocked, insufficient, or intentionally withheld irrigation event and is strongest in the zone supplied by that event or emitter. | In one controlled flowering experiment, visible wilt followed sustained drying and was accompanied by veinal chlorosis that began on older leaves and occurred less strongly on newer leaves across the plant; this is study-specific, not a universal color signature. | Sustained measured deficit can reduce leaf area, shoot expansion, total biomass, or seed/flower yield even when acute wilt is weak or delayed. | Cultivars can differ in stomatal closure, midday relative water content, wilting score, leaf retention, and recovery, so matched-plant context carries more weight than a generic droop class. | After careful rehydration, water status and posture may improve while photosynthesis or growth remains depressed; different recovery rates support a temporal water-response link but do not exclude coexisting injury.
exclusions: Do not label drought from one wilted, chlorotic, curled, or drooping image without a plant-linked moisture measurement and irrigation timeline. | If the root zone is adequately moist at representative center, edge, and depth locations while wilt persists, investigate other causes rather than assuming hidden drought. | Measure root-zone EC and source-water/fertilizer history because elevated salts can create osmotic stress even when volumetric water content appears adequate. | Exclude overwatering or hypoxia using moisture history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; drought and hypoxia can produce overlapping canopy wilt. | Inspect roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, necrotic, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain laboratory confirmation when Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or vascular disease remains plausible. | Record air temperature, leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow because high atmospheric demand or heat/light injury can change midday leaf posture without a primary soil-water deficit. | Inspect intact root-ball geometry and irrigation wetting because root binding, hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, blocked emitters, and small root volume can create localized water shortage with distinct corrective needs. | Exclude broken stems, girdling, transplant damage, pest injury, and normal cultivar or circadian leaf posture using crown inspection, organism scouting, matched controls, and time-of-day replication.
lookAlikes: Normal cultivar-specific or circadian leaf posture | High-temperature or high-VPD midday depression | Excess light or radiant-heat stress | Salinity / elevated root-zone EC stress | Root-zone hypoxia / overwatering | Pythium root rot | Fusarium or Rhizoctonia crown/root disease | Vascular wilt or stem/crown injury | Root binding / container-restriction stress | Hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, or blocked emitter | Root-knot nematodes or root-feeding insects | Transplant shock or mechanical root loss | Potassium or nitrogen deficiency with marginal/older-leaf symptoms | Camera angle, lens perspective, or time-of-day mismatch
confirmation: Assign a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy from fixed front and side positions plus representative fan leaves, substrate surface, container, emitter, drainage, and root-zone context with a metric scale and neutral color reference. | Measure volumetric water content or a validated medium-appropriate moisture proxy at multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions; log calibrated method, timestamp, last irrigation, applied volume, runoff, and the crop-specific baseline. | Repeat leaf-angle or posture images at the same time of day and camera geometry before deficit, during the suspected event, immediately before rehydration, and after rehydration; compare a matched same-cultivar irrigated plant. | Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at each capture so atmospheric demand can be separated from root-zone water availability. | Measure root-zone EC and pH, inspect emitter output and wetting uniformity, and document intact root-ball volume and boundary condition before disturbing roots. | Inspect roots, crown, and stem cross-sections for decay, lesions, odor, sloughing, galls, insects, girdling, and internal discoloration; send plant-linked samples for pathogen or nematode testing when indicated. | Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, sensor-unlinked, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed class and every automated training split.
immediateActions: Verify root-zone moisture, emitter function, wetting uniformity, EC, and drainage before applying water solely because the canopy appears wilted. | Preserve pre-correction images and measurements, then rehydrate conservatively according to medium and root condition while monitoring runoff and avoiding abrupt saturation of a compromised root zone. | Segregate or flag plants with root/crown decay, vascular discoloration, galls, or insects for diagnostic review rather than treating them as simple drought.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented delivery failure, insufficient volume/frequency, hydrophobicity, root-volume mismatch, or excessive atmospheric demand using production-system-specific measurements rather than a universal schedule. | Trend moisture, leaf posture, water status where available, EC, new growth, and root health after correction; persistent decline requires reassessment for salinity, hypoxia, structural injury, and disease. | Do not intentionally reproduce a published drought endpoint as a corrective or production recipe; controlled experimental stress thresholds are not validated as universal safe practices.
prevention: Build cultivar-, stage-, container-, substrate-, and environment-specific irrigation baselines from calibrated measurements and plant-linked observations. | Audit emitter output, pressure, wetting footprint, drainage, root volume, substrate rewetting behavior, and sensor placement before high-demand periods. | Use fixed-view, fixed-time healthy reference captures so normal circadian and cultivar posture can be distinguished from a developing water deficit.
warnings: Do not use one wilted photograph as proof of drought; retain it only as an unconfirmed visual lead until plant-linked water evidence and exclusions are available. | Wilting, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, slow growth, and rehydration response are supportive but not specific; drought remains an exposure-linked diagnosis. | The approximately 11-day drying period, -1.5 MPa plant-water-potential endpoint, and roughly 52% leaf-angle change came from one controlled flowering chemovar and must not be used as universal thresholds. | Hemp cultivars differ substantially in soil-drying and VPD responses, and observation time changes apparent wilting; a model must not learn one canopy posture as genotype-independent drought ground truth. | Published effects on cannabinoid concentration, biomass, and yield vary by genotype, severity, stage, and protocol; this diagnostic profile does not recommend intentional drought stress. | No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis drought progression image or verified diagnostic video with reusable item-level rights was located for this batch; publisher figures remain citations only and media stays empty.

name: Salinity / elevated root-zone EC stress
summary: Salinity/high-EC stress is an exposure-response diagnosis in which measured dissolved salts coincide with impaired Cannabis growth, physiology, or yield. EC reports total ionic conductivity but not which ions caused it: direct Cannabis experiments produced different responses when EC was raised with NaCl, concentrated nutrients, hydroponic solution, or aquaponic solution. Brown tips, chlorosis, wilt, and necrosis are therefore nonspecific and require plant-linked EC trends, solution composition, pH, moisture, roots, and matched controls.
affectedParts: irrigation water, nutrient solution, substrate, or root zone | root system | sampled leaves of documented age and canopy position | shoot tips and whole canopy | stems, leaves, inflorescences, biomass, and yield secondarily
stages: seedling | vegetative | flower | all production stages with a measured saline or concentrated-nutrient exposure
indicators: Measured irrigation or root-zone EC is elevated relative to the established crop baseline while growth declines | Growth suppression occurs together with a documented saline or high-salt root-zone exposure | Leaf nutrient imbalance appears after a measured salinity increase rather than an isolated single-element withholding pattern | Repeated plant-linked measurements show EC rising before or with reduced canopy expansion, leaf chlorophyll index, biomass accumulation, or yield relative to a matched same-cultivar control. | The affected distribution follows a documented solution, tank, irrigation zone, emitter, recirculation loop, container, or substrate-extraction pattern rather than a random lesion pattern. | Water, nutrient-solution, substrate-extract, or tissue chemistry identifies the ions or fertilizer concentration that produced the conductivity; EC alone does not identify sodium, chloride, or any single nutrient. | Visible leaf necrosis may appear under severe NaCl exposure, but one Early Haze rockwool trial observed it only at its two highest NaCl EC treatments while growth or yield effects occurred without that sign. | Direct studies show that production system and salt composition alter the response: hydroponic and aquaponic solutions differed under the same NaCl treatments, and nutrient-raised EC differed from NaCl-raised EC.
exclusions: Do not label salinity or “nutrient burn” from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting without a plant-linked EC measurement and exposure history. | If EC is stable within the established crop baseline and no saline, concentrated-fertilizer, source-water, recirculation, or accumulation pathway is documented, investigate another cause. | Measure root-zone water content across representative center, edge, and depth positions because simple drought, preferential wetting, or a failed emitter can resemble osmotic stress. | Exclude overwatering and hypoxia with irrigation history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; a wet root zone does not prove salts are causal. | Measure root-zone pH and review tissue or solution chemistry because abnormal pH or a verified single-element deficiency or toxicity can create a similar canopy pattern. | Inspect intact roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, galled, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain organism confirmation when root disease or nematodes remain plausible. | Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, airflow, and recent spray history to exclude heat, light, high atmospheric demand, droplet, and contact injury. | Check root-ball geometry, substrate compaction, container temperature, and root restriction because small or uneven root volume can produce localized water and nutrient stress without primary salinity.
lookAlikes: Drought / water-deficit stress | Root-zone hypoxia / overwatering | Abnormal root-zone pH or mixed nutrient lockout | Potassium deficiency | Magnesium deficiency | Nitrogen toxicity or excessive ammonium | Boron, manganese, or other nutrient toxicity | Pythium or Fusarium root/crown disease | Root-knot nematodes | Root binding / container-restriction stress | High-temperature or high-VPD stress | Light or lamp-proximity injury | Foliar spray, disinfectant, or contact injury | Normal late-flowering senescence
confirmation: Calibrate the EC and pH meters and record input water, mixed solution, and representative root-zone or leachate values with the extraction method, temperature compensation, units, date, and plant or irrigation-zone identity. | Sample multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions or multiple emitters and containers; compare the trend with the established production baseline and a matched same-cultivar unaffected control. | Document fertilizer products, mixing order and concentration, source-water analysis, sodium and chloride inputs, irrigation volume, drainage fraction, recirculation history, evaporation, and any tank or dosing fault. | When the salt source is uncertain, obtain solution, substrate-extract, and tissue analysis for sodium, chloride, and relevant macro- and micronutrients; do not infer ion composition from EC. | Measure root-zone moisture, pH, and temperature and record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at the same time as each visual capture. | Inspect and photograph the intact root ball, crown, drainage pattern, emitter placement, and root color and firmness; use diagnostic testing when disease, nematodes, or vascular injury remains plausible. | Capture fixed whole-plant front and side views plus top, upper-leaf, lower-leaf, margin, underside, root-zone, meter-display, and source-label views at the same time of day before exposure, during the EC rise, before correction, and during recovery. | Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, meter-unlinked, composition-unknown, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed salinity class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Verify the reading with a calibrated meter and a medium-appropriate sampling method before changing fertilizer or irrigation. | Record moisture, pH, roots, solution composition, and the affected irrigation zone before corrective actions erase the exposure evidence.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented salt source, dosing fault, source-water problem, recirculation accumulation, or root-zone concentration with a crop- and medium-specific plan; this record does not prescribe a universal flush volume or target EC. | Trend input and root-zone EC, moisture, pH, new growth, and matched controls after correction; investigate coexisting root or environmental injury if recovery does not follow.
prevention: Trend calibrated input and root-zone EC with consistent sampling methods, units, temperature handling, crop stage, and irrigation-zone identity. | Account separately for source-water ions, fertilizer formulation, drainage, recirculation, evaporation, substrate, container size, cultivar, and crop stage when establishing baselines and alerts.
warnings: EC is a conductivity measurement, not an ion identity: the same EC can be produced by NaCl or by different nutrient mixtures with different Cannabis responses. | The published 1.8 to 12 mS/cm, 1 to 40 mM NaCl, and 0.4 to 6 dS/m treatments are study-specific exposures, not universal safe, toxic, correction, or training-label thresholds. | Do not diagnose “nutrient burn” or salinity from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting alone; photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.20. | Visible necrosis was restricted to the highest NaCl treatments in one Early Haze rockwool experiment, while other measured effects occurred without that sign; absence or presence of necrosis is not decisive. | The evidence spans one drug-type chemovar, Early Haze, and Felina 32 fiber hemp under distinct hydroponic, aquaponic, rockwool, mesocosm, nutrient, NaCl, and biostimulant conditions; cultivar and system transfer requires human review. | No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis salinity progression image or verified diagnostic video met the acquisition standard, so media remains an explicit gap and automated training eligibility remains false.

name: Hop latent viroid
summary: A systemic viroid whose Cannabis expression ranges from asymptomatic infection to genotype- and stage-dependent dudding, poor rooting, stunting, abnormal foliage, and reduced inflorescence or trichome development. Appearance is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis: a ground-truth HLVd label requires a validated molecular result linked to the sampled plant.
affectedParts: rooted cuttings and adventitious roots | root system | stems, branches, and internodes | young and expanded foliage across the canopy | whole-plant architecture | inflorescence stems and flower tissues | glandular trichomes | propagation stock and reproductive material
stages: asymptomatic stock or mother plant | propagation and rooting | vegetative growth | flowering and inflorescence development | field growth with symptoms potentially clearer from mid-season onward
indicators: Short internodes | Brittle stems or leaves | Stunted growth | No visible abnormality: infected stock plants and young rooted cuttings can be asymptomatic, so a normal-looking frame is not an HLVd-negative label. | Poor or delayed root emergence in cuttings taken from an infected mother, evaluated against same-age clean comparators; weak rooting is nonspecific and requires root-zone and pathogen exclusions. | Whole-plant stunting or reduced vigor relative to genetically matched, same-age plants under the same environment rather than an isolated small plant without context. | Shorter internodes, smaller leaves, or compact architecture distributed across new growth; severity can vary by genotype and must not be confused with stable genetic stature or deliberate training. | Mild leaf curl, mottling, yellow patterning, generalized yellowing, or misshapen leaves; no single color or leaf-shape pattern is consistently present or specific to HLVd. | Brittle stems or branches affecting otherwise intact shoots; a single snapped or trained branch is not evidence of systemic infection. | During flowering, reduced inflorescence-stem growth, smaller or poorly developed flowers, and yellowing or darkening of leaves surrounding flowers can occur in susceptible genotypes. | Reduced glandular-trichome development may appear as lower resin coverage at matched magnification and maturity, but trichome density or head size alone cannot distinguish HLVd from genetics, maturity, lighting, temperature, handling, or imaging differences.
exclusions: Do not assign HLVd from stunting, short internodes, yellowing, leaf curl, brittle growth, poor roots, small flowers, low resin, or any combination of visible signs without a plant-linked validated molecular result. | Measured root-zone pH, EC, moisture, oxygenation, or nutrient correction explains the change and the suspect plant is molecularly negative on appropriately collected and timed samples. | Root and crown examination plus laboratory work identifies Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, root aphids, fungus-gnat larvae, root binding, or another cause of poor rooting and decline without HLVd detection. | Magnified inspection confirms broad mites, hemp russet mites, thrips, or spider mites that account for distorted or mottled new growth, with no supporting HLVd assay. | Compact stature, short internodes, or low trichome coverage remains stable in a molecularly negative clonal lineage under healthy measured conditions, supporting a genetic or developmental trait rather than infection. | Yellowing follows the older-to-younger distribution and timing expected for measured nitrogen deficiency or normal late-cycle senescence, and properly sampled tissue is HLVd-negative. | A single branch is brittle, wilted, or undersized after topping, wind, abrasion, constriction, or another documented mechanical event while the rest of the plant and new growth remain normal. | One negative leaf sample is not a universal exclusion when sampling timing, tissue distribution, extraction quality, or inhibition is uncertain; use the laboratory sampling plan and retest roots or multiple positions when advised.
lookAlikes: Genetic dwarfism, compact architecture, or cultivar-specific low vigor | Normal late-flowering senescence or cultivar-specific fade | Nitrogen, sulfur, iron, magnesium, or other nutrient deficiency | Excess fertilizer, salinity, or root-zone pH stress | Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or other root/crown disease | Root binding, waterlogging, drought, or low root-zone oxygen | Broad mite or hemp russet mite injury | Thrips or spider-mite feeding injury | Beet curly top virus, phytoplasma, or another systemic pathogen | Heat, high light, photoperiod, or plant-growth-regulator injury | Mechanical damage, topping, or training response | Normal genetic or maturity-driven differences in flower and trichome development
confirmation: Submit plant-linked samples to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory for a validated HLVd RT-PCR, RT-qPCR, or equivalent sequence-specific assay; a photo, video, growth pattern, or trichome image cannot confirm infection. | Follow the laboratory’s current sampling instructions. Because HLVd distribution can vary across leaves and roots, record the tissue type and canopy position and consider paired root plus upper, middle, or lower foliage samples when the laboratory recommends them. | For young rooted cuttings, roots may provide a more consistent testing target than leaves; Oregon State reports that roots can test positive about two weeks after cuttings are made, while young plants may remain visually normal above ground. | Retest when an assay is negative but sample timing, tissue choice, extraction quality, inhibition, chain of custody, or symptoms remain concerning; do not reinterpret one poorly contextualized negative leaf as proof that the whole plant is clean. | Pair molecular testing with same-genotype, same-age, same-environment clean controls and serial whole-plant measurements so reductions in height, internode length, root emergence, flower development, or trichome appearance are not attributed across unmatched plants. | Inspect and document roots, crown, leaf undersides, growing tips, root-zone pH/EC/moisture, irrigation history, light/temperature, and recent training or chemical exposure to evaluate common non-HLVd causes and possible mixed problems. | For image/video ground truth, preserve the plant ID, cultivar or genotype, sample date, sampled tissue and position, assay method and result, symptom date, and source group. Keep unlinked, symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, and assay-panel-only captures out of the confirmed class.
immediateActions: Flag and physically segregate suspect propagation material while results are pending; stop taking or distributing cuttings, pollen, seed, or tools from the suspect plant. | Use separate or decontaminated cutting tools and handling equipment according to a validated facility protocol, and avoid moving sap from suspect plants to clean stock. | Capture matched whole-plant, canopy, growing-tip, root, and flower views before destructive sampling, but label the observation “HLVd suspect” rather than confirmed.
correctivePlan: Base removal, retention, retesting, and sanitation decisions on the confirmed laboratory result and a written facility disease protocol. | If HLVd is not detected, continue the differential workup for root pathogens, mites, nutrient and root-zone problems, systemic viruses or phytoplasmas, genetic traits, and maturity. | Do not promise that a visible recovery, treatment, or single cleaning product eradicates HLVd; verify clean status through the testing and sanitation program.
prevention: Use traceable mother stock, incoming clones, pollen, and seed that have been tested under an appropriate sampling program. | Separate untested propagation material from clean stock and maintain plant IDs linking mothers, cuttings, assay results, dates, and work areas. | Clean sap and plant debris from tools, benches, irrigation components, and equipment, then apply a viroid protocol validated for the specific surface, product concentration, contact time, and workflow.
warnings: HLVd cannot be confirmed or excluded from visible symptoms; infected plants may be asymptomatic and visually abnormal plants may have many other causes. | Growth reduction, flower loss, THC or terpene change, and trichome effects are genotype- and experiment-dependent; do not apply study percentages to an individual plant or cultivar. | One tissue or canopy position may test negative while another tests positive, so sampling context and assay quality must remain attached to every laboratory label. | An RT-PCR signal establishes target RNA in the sampled material; sanitation experiments based on loss of an amplifiable band do not automatically prove every treated surface or plant material is noninfectious. | The two Oregon State hemp figures below are metadata-only references. Their creators are credited, but no explicit reuse license is stated; do not display, copy, modify, or use them for automated training without written permission. | Keep every symptom-only, unlinked assay, detached-leaf-only, unmatched-comparator, low-resolution trichome, or uncertain-tissue sample flagged for human review.

name: Beet curly top virus disease
summary: A beet-leafhopper-vectored viral disease of field-grown hemp that can produce uneven stunting, bushy or shortened shoots, twisted and upward-curled young leaves, and pale-green, yellow, mosaic, or fully chlorotic foliage.
affectedParts: young and expanding leaves | shoot tips | stems and internodes | buds | whole plant
stages: seedling | vegetative | pre-flower | flower
indicators: Stunted or bushy plant architecture | Twisted, puckered, or upward-curled young leaves | Pale-green to yellow new foliage | Yellow mosaic or generalized chlorosis | Shortened stem growth | Symptomatic shoots beside apparently healthy shoots on the same plant
exclusions: Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in protected new growth | Distortion follows a documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure pattern | Symptoms are uniform only on the hottest or brightest canopy surface and measured environmental stress explains the distribution | Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient pattern without twisted new shoots | A validated laboratory assay is negative on properly collected tissue and another cause is confirmed
lookAlikes: Tomato spotted wilt virus | Broad mite | Hemp russet mite | Plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury | Heat or light stress | Micronutrient or root-zone disorder | Genetic or chimeric variegation
