confirmation: Do not confirm BCTV from an image or from beet-leafhopper presence; submit representative symptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory using a validated BCTV-targeted molecular assay. | Sample newly symptomatic shoots rather than only old damaged leaves, and include an apparently healthy comparison when the laboratory protocol allows. | Ask the laboratory to consider other viruses or mixed infection when symptoms or assay results do not fully agree; BCTV can occur in mixed strain or mixed pathogen infections. | Record field position, onset date, affected growth stage, nearby weed hosts, and beet-leafhopper observations to support epidemiological interpretation without treating them as proof of infection.
immediateActions: Mark and isolate suspect propagation material; stop taking or distributing cuttings until laboratory results are available. | Scout the crop, field edges, leaf undersides, and nearby weeds for beet leafhoppers and additional symptomatic plants. | Prevent unverified symptom images from being assigned a virus ground-truth label.
correctivePlan: Base roguing or retention decisions on laboratory confirmation and the facility or field disease protocol. | Manage beet-leafhopper exposure with locally recommended legal practices; vector control does not cure an infected plant. | Continue monitoring because visible symptoms may vary among shoots or appear to recede.
prevention: Use tested propagation material and maintain source records. | Monitor beet leafhoppers from spring onward with crop inspection and field-edge trapping appropriate to the production system. | Reduce unmanaged weed and volunteer hosts around field borders using legal, agronomically appropriate practices.
warnings: Visual symptoms are not specific enough to confirm a virus. | A beet leafhopper on a plant does not establish that the insect or plant carries BCTV. | The two institutional hemp photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden from the public gallery and prohibited from automated training.

name: Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia
summary: A persistently saturated root zone can suppress Cannabis root elongation, leaf expansion, relative chlorophyll, gas exchange, and biomass; the canopy response overlaps drought, nutrient, transplant, and root-disease injury, so exposure measurements are required.
affectedParts: root system | whole canopy | expanding leaves | reproductive canopy
stages: transplant establishment | vegetative | reproductive
indicators: Root zone remains saturated or stands in water across repeated observations | Whole-plant growth and canopy expansion slow relative to a matched healthy plant | Root system is shorter or has less new growth than a matched control | Canopy greenness declines over time rather than forming discrete lesions | Leaf-area development and biomass accumulation remain depressed after drainage
exclusions: Container weight or substrate-water measurement shows the root zone is dry rather than saturated | The pattern is restricted to one mechanically damaged branch | Discrete leaf lesions, fungal growth, vascular discoloration, root galls, or organisms provide a better causal explanation | Roots are brown, soft, or decayed and a laboratory test identifies Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or another pathogen | Measured salinity or pH is outside the crop target and explains the distribution better | Only canopy posture is available without irrigation, drainage, root, or time-series context
lookAlikes: Water shortage or drought | Pythium root rot | Phytophthora root or crown rot | Fusarium wilt or crown disease | High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability | Nitrogen deficiency | Poor transplant root establishment
confirmation: Document irrigation volume and timing, drainage duration, runoff, standing water, container weight, or calibrated substrate-water content across time; a canopy photograph alone cannot confirm waterlogging. | Compare the entire plant and cleaned root system with a healthy plant of the same cultivar, age, medium, and stage, recording root length, active root tips, leaf-area expansion, and recovery after drainage is restored. | Measure root-zone pH and EC because salinity and nutrient availability can produce overlapping canopy decline. | If roots or crowns are discolored, soft, necrotic, or decayed, submit representative root and crown tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory before assigning an abiotic-only label.
immediateActions: Stop adding unnecessary irrigation and remove standing water while preserving a documented sample of the pre-correction root-zone condition. | Separate drainage and runoff from healthy plants when infectious root disease remains possible. | Inspect roots, emitters, drain paths, and neighboring containers before choosing a correction.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured cause of persistent saturation, such as blocked drainage, excessive shot size or frequency, poor container drainage, compacted media, or flooding. | Return irrigation gradually to a measured dryback pattern appropriate to the crop stage and medium, then score only new growth and root recovery. | Use laboratory results and locally legal crop protocols if a root pathogen is confirmed; drainage correction alone does not establish or cure a pathogen diagnosis.
prevention: Record irrigation input, runoff, container weight or substrate water content, and dryback duration instead of relying on a fixed calendar. | Use matched healthy controls and photograph the whole plant, root zone, and cleaned roots across time. | Keep drainage paths functional and prevent shared runoff from moving between containers.
warnings: Reduced growth, pale foliage, or leaf posture is not specific to excess water and must not be used as image-only ground truth. | The controlled waterlogging results come from one Cannabis genotype and defined seven-to-21-day treatments; symptom timing and severity should not be generalized as universal thresholds. | Brown or decayed roots cannot safely be labeled abiotic hypoxia without excluding Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, and other root diseases. | No symptom photograph with adequate Cannabis-specific confirmation and reusable provenance was admitted in this batch.
